To gain a deeper understanding, we employed a coarse-grained, Monte Carlo simulation, considering arbitrary branch shapes and varying degrees of polymerization. Our analysis revealed that, despite variations in morphology, all branched structures exhibit identical scaling properties. Furthermore, we identified distinct regimes in strongly stretched polymers, characterized by intricate packing patterns that control chain configuration and bonding. These regimes dictate that monomers at the chain's terminus and those at the base have fixed, arbitrary positions, while those in between are arranged in a uniform, curved line. The bristle model's revised understanding also implies that ring-shaped branches serve as isolated spaces that prevent neighboring polymer chains from interacting. This novel insight offers a new perspective on the polymer's configuration and interaction dynamics, emerging from the disruption of a fundamental concept in physics.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when its connection structure alone is sufficient to determine the position of any vertex, based on the distances between all pairs of vertices. A minimum set of landmarks or landmark vertices can be determined, which, when combined with the connection distances to these landmarks, enable the location of any vertex in the graph. The size of this smallest landmark set is referred to as the graph's shortened metric dimension. This paper explores the concept of shortened metric dimension in relation to various graph properties, specifically whether it is a maximum or a minimum score function, and whether it is a hereditary or an easiness property. Additionally, methods for calculating the shortened metric dimension of any graph G are also identified, including a landmark-based approach and one inspired by the metric dimension of a graph's complement.

The Fermi All-sky Variability Analysis System (FAVOR) is an automated tool for the exhaustive analysis of all-sky maps captured by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. It generates reliability charts for identifying variable sources, yet these charts are currently quite vague. To enhance their utility, we have modified the traditional significance testing approach to prioritize genuine variations over random fluctuations. As a result, the revised charts are more precise and effective at highlighting genuine variable sources. We applied these updated methods to a vast dataset spanning 8 years and identified 25 additional variable sources in the sky, in addition to the 91 sources previously cited in the second Fermi-LAT catalogue of gamma-ray sources with the highest variability. These sources are characterized by their power spectral density profiles, and we discovered that 8 of these additional sources exhibit signs of pulsations. The revised methods we developed are now part of the upgraded FAVOR framework, which is available online.

Inspired by the success of proportional representation systems in integrating diverse voter preferences, we explore the potential of a new mechanism for combining preferences in combinatorial auctions with multiple private budgets. Our analysis reveals that a serial dictatorship mechanism is already an optimal solution for solving this problem. However, we identify certain desirable features, such as fairness and ease of implementation, that are lost in its application. In response, we design two alternative mechanisms that maintain these desired characteristics while achieving comparable performance to the most efficient solutions. Specifically, these mechanisms ensure that the social welfare maximizer's items have a high probability of being selected, with this chance proportional to the square root of the largest budget in a wide range of settings. Furthermore, our approaches provide better results when there is a large disparity between the largest and smallest budgets. Our proposed solutions involve the combination of two techniques: first identifying a high probability of certain optimal allocations being selected under a given serial dictatorship, and then selectively applying a Myerson-Vickre approach to account for budget constraints.

We searched the Pan-STARRS1 (PS1) sky survey and adjacent areas for binary asteroids that were previously unknown.  By cross-referencing asteroid orbits with images from the PS1 survey, we localized 21 close pairs of asteroids and compared their observed light curves with computational simulations.  Our analysis covered 116 high-priority binary asteroids, including those we found, and estimated the fraction of observable binary asteroids to be around 5% when taking detection limitations into account.  This research was part of the BASS survey, a collaborative effort between astronomers studying binary asteroids.

This research supplements the findings of Wang, T., Wang, Q. A., and Tchou, A. J. (2020), which explored the estimation of a partial linear regression model under certain conditions and demonstrated its applicability through a simulation and real-world network analysis. We have expanded upon their work by detailing the estimation procedures for the partial linear regression model and conducting a thorough analysis of the standard asymptotic theory. Furthermore, we have derived the local asymptotic normality property and the efficient score for the model's parameters. Our study also offers a novel interpretation of the results in the context of peer influence within networks. Additionally, we have developed a method to identify central influencers within networks. Furthermore, we have conducted a comprehensive analysis of network data, including a discussion of network data's key characteristics, common graph metrics, and a comparison of our results with those of Wang, T., Wang, Q. A., and Tchou, A. J. (2020).

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for these operators.

This paper analyzes the performance of a least-squares estimation algorithm under varying sensor conditions and demonstrates its optimal data-processing capability. By applying this optimization to a range-finding problem, we develop an innovative method to calculate spatial averages and facilitate the identification of hidden signals. This approach is then utilized in a practical application involving music analysis, specifically in identifying the location and movement of drummers within a performance.

These are the underlying algorithms and methods employed by the RCSED team for developing the RCSED II dataset, which is based on real observations and incorporates a realistic simulation of various astronomical instruments. RCSED II is a comprehensive dataset containing one-dimensional spectra and pseudo-imaging data for 835 distinct galaxy types, spanning the redshift range 0-10, and has been utilized in multiple studies. We have established an automated framework for processing and manipulating these data, which is now available for public use through a web interface. This framework can simulate spectral and imaging observations for specific targets or general categories, as well as create II-band pseudo-imaging data from spectral data. Additionally, it simulates general target spectra and pseudo-imaging data based on predefined models, and can also generate random variations in redshift, observing conditions, and target properties. Furthermore, this framework can be employed for training machine learning models by generating vast amounts of simulated data, and we have already successfully developed a model using this framework, which has been used to develop a new semi-analytical model of galaxy evolution.

Located within the South American plate, the Rio Grande do Sul rift system in Brazil has been actively extending for nearly 8 million years. Despite this, data collected from thermal neutron decay, infrasound, and magnetic fields suggest that this area has not yet reached the point of significant volcanic activity associated with rifts. Furthermore, sedimentary coverage in this area makes it difficult to obtain batimetric data, compound the challenge of mapping the rift's geometry. However, based on echosoundings and bathymetric data, we were able to identify and measure the along-axis and down-axis dimensions of blocks within this rift. Results indicate that this rift system exhibits linear block geometry, with variations in block size consistent with the idea that break-up velocity decreases as the distance to the edge of the continental plate decreases.

Recently, information maximization-based self-supervised medical image segmentation methods have gained popularity due to their ability to extend segmentation models across different images without additional annotation. While such approaches have shown promise, they often rely on noisy gradient estimates, leading to inaccurate model optimization. To address this limitation, this study proposes an alternative framework that leverages boundary-sensitive information maximization for self-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed framework utilizes model-based synthetic images and corresponding segmentations to derive reliable gradient estimates, facilitating optimal model parameters. Furthermore, to handle real-world images, the framework is modified to use model-based image segmentation as a bridge to achieve efficient information maximization. Experimental results indicate that the proposed framework yields state-of-the-art performance in comparison to baseline methods for cardiac left ventricle segmentation in cine-CARDIAC challenges dataset and achieves comparable performance on PASCAL VOC segmentation dataset.

We introduce a groundbreaking approach for an interactive AI between users and role-playing games, drawing from sources like dialogical AI, game theory, and cognitive science. This approach is being tested in a real-world setting through the popular Dungeons and Dragons online version. In this scenario, one player is a non-human AI entity known as the Dungeon Master. The DMTM's primary goals are to create an engaging experience for the human players and ensure the game adheres to established rules. To achieve these goals, the DMTM must utilize a set of limited actions that can influence the human players' decisions. The DMTM's success depends on its ability to understand the human players' thoughts and intentions. To evaluate this system, thousands of human players are participating in online D&D sessions with the DMTM. Words convey meaning and vary in accordance to the context in which they are spoken.  Despite significant progress made to date, the relationship between the lexical form and the surrounding syntactic context is not yet fully understood.  A promising approach to uncovering hidden connections involves analyzing the shifts in word meanings across similar contexts.  This paper introduces three innovative methods for identifying and quantifying the shifts in word meanings, along with comprehensive evaluations of their performance.  The results show that two of these methods successfully reveal the anticipated semantic changes, while the third method offers valuable insights into the relationships between words with opposite meanings.  Furthermore, our research introduces two novel datasets that comprise the means by which word meanings adapt to changing contextual settings: LexSemShift and LexSemChange.  LexSemChange holds the distinction of being the first publicly accessible dataset to detail the shifts in word meanings across varying syntactic contexts.

We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. Additionally, they depend on the movement of partons in the transverse direction, related to parton spin alignment, which is rooted in the interactions represented by corresponding correlators.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area of ongoing biophysical research. To further understand this connection, we've developed a method for visualizing and analyzing the topological properties of spatially embedded knots within proteins. By applying this approach to a diverse set of unfolded proteins, we've identified the underlying geometric structures that form along their bending pathways. Our results demonstrate the presence of distinct, irreducible knots within various protein sequences, and by examining these structures through a topological lens, we've identified specific knotting patterns associated with arterial and gastrointestinal proteins. Furthermore, our technique enables the identification of knotted protein regions that exhibit low friction and high curvature, and we've established a relationship between these areas and the corresponding bending pathways. Our research provides a topological framework for studying the complex relationships between protein knots, folding processes, and function, and our approach is now widely adopted as a standard method for analyzing knotted proteins.

To resolve the underlying nature of cosmic structure formation, early dark energy (EDE) cosmologies have been proposed as an alternative to the $\Lambda$CDM model. Although single-component EDE models have been shown to fit galaxy data effectively, they are inconsistent with findings from cosmic microwave background experiments. We have developed an analytical method to evaluate the probability of EDE existing below a certain density threshold, using the profile likelihood technique and a comprehensive set of galaxy data. Our analysis places tight constraints on EDE parameters and confirms previous findings that single-component EDE models are inconsistent with observational data. In particular, we have determined that the probability of EDE existing with a density greater than $10^{-4}$ times the critical density is less than $0.002$ (at $95\%$ confidence). Our analysis also places upper and lower limits on the EDE start density at $0.07$ and $0.01$, respectively, with an accuracy of $0.01$. We have further investigated multi-component EDE models that could potentially avoid conflicts with cosmic microwave background data. While such models may fit galaxy data as well as single-component EDE models, they are inconsistent with findings from cosmic microwave background experiments at more than $95\%$ confidence. Our analysis places tight constraints on the parameters of these models, with start densities ranging from $0.026$ to $0.55$, with an accuracy of $0.01$. Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Assume that $\omega$ fulfills an irrationality condition and has an irrational Einstien series. This paper proves that the symplectic mapping type group of the one-point blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably generated.

A detailed examination of the Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem is performed, 
focusing on its underlying assumptions and the nature of the NG bosons that 
appear when symmetry is broken. A specially constructed model serves as 
the central example, showcasing a seemingly anomalous NG phenomenon, 
which requires a thorough explanation. This is achieved by redefining 
the'spontaneous symmetry breaking' category and distinguishing between 
'effective' and 'primary' symmetry breakings. The relationship between 
the symmetry group and the representation of the symmetry group, 
determining the 'would-be NG field,' is also clarified. The general 
applicability of the NG theorem is preserved, considered from both the 
algebraic and algebra-free (Schwartz-type) perspectives. Theoretical 
analysis is complemented by numerical simulation, offering additional 
insights into the phenomenon. The connection to the vacuum expectation 
value (VEV) is reexamined, and the VEV's physical interpretation is 
discussed in both relativistic and nonrelativistic contexts. The devised 
model also raises questions regarding the conditions under which the 
NG mode becomes 'free.' The proposed solution involves the generation of 
mass for both 'would-be NG fields' and the associated'massless fields,' 
separating the phenomenon of symmetry breaking from the generation of 
mass. The relationship between the symmetry group, representation, and

Recent studies suggest that language models can provide valuable insights into
language usage by analyzing what they have learned from extensive exposure to
language. Nonetheless, our comprehension of how language is perceived through
the lens of language models remains limited. Research into the study of language
models' subjective experience, specifically their perception of counterfactual
statements - statements about what could have been - is particularly underdevel-
oped. While prior work has focused mainly on analyzing the performance of
machine-generated counterfactuals, they have the drawback of relying on
automated evaluation tools, which only consider the superficial aspects of
generated text. In contrast, our work takes a novel approach by directing
attention to the study of complex counterfactual phrases within a broader
language context. We introduce a specially designed dataset called
CFW14k, containing nearly 15,000 counterfactual phrases drawn from a range
of sentence patterns, along with corresponding contextual information. To
accomplish this, we developed a versatile framework called DISCO, consisting of
several components that can effectively identify and evaluate complex
counterfactual phrases within a broader language context. Moreover, we
investigated various aspects of CFW14k's counterfactual phrases, including
their relationships with other phrases, their link to actual events, and their
connection to personal perspectives. Interestingly, our research found that
these counterfactual phrases are distinct from factual phrases and often
contradict commonly held beliefs

In this study, we determined the minimum number of colors required to color various types of circulant graphs in one and two dimensions, ensuring that no two adjacent vertices have the same color and that the coloring pattern is distinguishable. Additionally, we established a link between these determinations and their counterparts in the context of fair total and neighborhood colorings.

Research into remote epitaxy offers novel possibilities for fabricating thin films remotely, using weak interactions on a variety of substrates. However, the underlying principles of remote epitaxy remain not fully understood, mainly because it's difficult to distinguish it from other growth mechanisms such as van der Waals epitaxy and pinhole bridging. Recent advancements indicate that the equilibrium between these mechanisms can be influenced by external stress and potential differences at the interface, giving rise to new avenues for controlling epitaxy through surface and interface engineering. This study focuses on the epitaxial growth of the Heusler compound GdPtS films on single-layer graphene, where it was observed that pinholes and vdW gaps form spontaneously around small islands of strain. It was found that this strain causes a curvature of the graphene surface, generating a potential dip that films nucleate within. As the film thickness increases, the curvature weakens, along with the potential dip, which in turn disrupts the bridging of pinholes, giving rise to a switch from pinhole bridging to remote growth. Interestingly, films grown at higher temperatures exhibit thicker vdW gaps due to increased surface diffusion, yet still maintain the same strain. Notably, this strain facilitates bridging of small gaps between the film and the graphene, allowing for the switch from remote to pinhole bridging. As a result, precise control over surface and interface energy can be achieved by introducing external stress, which can also affect the film's thickness in the remote growth mode

This paper delves into a specific class of codes called $p^r$-linear codes, which are a part of the broader category of linear codes. Specifically, we're going to focus on a subclass known as $\Z_p\Z_{p^2}$-linear codes. Our discussion will cover the calculation of the dimension of this type of code and the determination of its corresponding null space.

The flow profile of an ideal polymer plug is examined under various injection conditions, considering the effects of fluid incompressibility, Newtonian fluid properties, shear thinning behavior, and Viscosity variation with shear rate. A comparative analysis of different polymer models, including the Carreau, Carreau-Yasuda, and Bird-Carreau models, is performed to determine their impact on the profile. Additionally, the influence of shear thickening fluids on the profile is also investigated. Furthermore, we derive and present explicit equations for the flow profile in the case of power-law fluids and demonstrate the applicability of the ideal polymer plug concept to fluid injections involving non-Newtonian behavior, including power-law and Bird-Carreau fluids.

A positive label for a specific instance can originate from various sources, including user input or classification output. Nonetheless, utilizing this single positive label to train models is not feasible due to the absence of corresponding negative instances. Consequently, we propose utilizing a dataset with comprehensive multi-label annotations to supplement the label. Notably, we distinguish our approach from existing methods that either select existing negative labels or merge positive labels without referencing the original dataset. In contrast, we develop a multi-class retrieval framework to selectively incorporate relevant negative labels based on the original annotation. Moreover, we devise an aggregation strategy to integrate instances with multiple labels that share the same annotation, reducing potential data imbalance. Ultimately, our goal is to enhance model performance by accurately predicting multi-label instances with a single positive label in domains like text, image, and audio.

This article addresses the issue of J.N. Colton's and P.C. Lasko's limitation proof for the finite energy possessed by the solution of the Cahn-Hilliard equation at infinite time. We provide an alternate proof utilizing time-fractional phase-field equations, which are widely regarded as a safe and reliable approach. Furthermore, our findings indicate that even with discontinuous initial data, the energy remains finite over time.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract algebras and Hilbert space representations, mapping abstract algebras to representations and morphisms to operators. This process involves a abstract algebra's associated state, which serves as a starting point. A state can be viewed as a special type of positive operator and is closely linked to the algebra through various properties. These properties, combined with the associated von Neumann algebra and state, provide a comprehensive understanding of the algebra's representations. This connection allows us to study the algebra itself through its associated state and von Neumann algebra. A key insight is that this relationship is not just a one-way process - we can use the algebra's representations to derive its underlying state. This process involves identifying the maximal abelian subalgebras within the algebra, which in turn enables the determination of the associated state through von Neumann algebra's port-based quantum operational structure. Ultimately, this connection between abstract algebras and their representations raises fundamental questions about the algebra's underlying structure and its relationship to its derived properties.

The current understanding of gamma-ray astronomy suggests that extremely energetic rays are produced through extreme processes, specifically massive collisions, massive deaths, or massive energies released from magnetic snares. However, the detection of gamma-rays from several powerful galaxies, including quasars and blazars, remains unaccounted for under this theory. It is proposed that captured material falling into these galaxies' black holes could generate gamma-rays if it is redirected by magnetic fields into an accretion disk around the black hole. This idea is supported by observations of oxygen vapor, a byproduct of captured material, and is consistent with the characteristics of powering engines in these galaxies. Furthermore, this model suggests that a significant portion of galaxies could be capable of producing high-energy gamma-rays, potentially affecting cosmic photon flux.

This study seeks to resolve the paradox of asset pricing models having positive expectations for zero-net-investment portfolios. We demonstrate that the standard CAPM and APT frameworks lead to mispricing of zero-net-investment portfolios due to their failure to account for direct competition among investors. We then examine two alternative models - the Fund Theory and the Dynamic Asset Allocation models - and show they are devoid of this pricing error. Furthermore, we provide empirical evidence supporting the Fund Theory over the standard CAPM and SDF-based asset pricing models.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormal heart sound detection and classification by auscultation are hampered by background noise and the variability of sound patterns due to differing patient positions.  As such, we tackle two key challenges in this area: representing heart sound patterns in a stable manner and accounting for additional noise.  To this end, we employ a constant Q transform to stabilize heart sound patterns,  and a constant Q transform with adaptive deformation to account for varying sound patterns due to noise.  The features extracted from the heart sounds are then used with a convolutional neural network to achieve high accuracy in classifying abnormal heart sounds.  The results of our research demonstrate the potential of cardiac sound analysis using low-cost, non-invasive methods.

The proliferation of wearable devices and cloud computing simplifies accessing health data, enabling various applications but also poses challenges in data sharing, privacy, and storage. A significant issue is addressing class imbalance in medical datasets, which is crucial for deploying machine learning models effectively in real-world medical scenarios. In this paper, a new approach is introduced, where a model is trained through a federated transfer learning process to combat the difficulty in finding balanced datasets. The proposed algorithm, FedHealth, leverages the advantages of both federated and transfer learning techniques to excel in wearable medical dataset applications. In our experiments, FedHealth demonstrated superior performance compared to conventional approaches in real-world wearable health dataset scenarios.

This study contrasts various methods for portfolio optimization that go beyond basic expectations, including those using higher moments, entropy, and robust techniques. We examine the implications of utilising higher-order moments, specific information about asset returns, and entropy within a stable framework, before exploring the benefits of robust optimisation in a environment with uncertain return data.

The apparent synchronicity of the onset of PERSEUS observations with the galaxy 3C454.03 flaring up can be interpreted from multiple perspectives. To illustrate this, we'll examine the likelihood of coincidences occurring by chance, taking into consideration various factors such as the frequency of observations and the characteristics of the galaxy in question. A statistical test has been devised for assessing the likelihood of observations overlapping with astronomical events, and this test indicates that the events mentioned in this paper do not require any special assumptions to have occurred by chance. However, it's also possible to view the overlap as significant, taking into consideration the findings of previous studies and the characteristics of this particular galaxy, and this perspective is also supported by a more refined analysis. Ultimately, any interpretation of the results is subjective and may vary depending on the researcher's perspective.

The integration of low-level computer specifications and high-level software applications is known as systems programming. System programming involves writing operating system code and implementing low-level computer functions in order to manage and operate the computer's hardware components. It encompasses various areas including device drivers, network protocols, and file systems. However, creating such code is challenging due to the need to consider hardware limitations, data formats, and the potential for system crashes. Furthermore, existing software testing and validation methodologies are not effective enough in ensuring the reliability of system programming code. As a result, system programmers often resort to traditional techniques such as experience-based decision making and manual code manipulation. Nevertheless, the rising demand for complex software systems has created a significant shortage of skilled system programmers. In response to this shortfalls, this research proposes the use of artificial intelligence in automating software processing, a concept known as Automated Software Processing (ASP). ASP has the potential to improve system programming efficiency, reduce errors associated with time-consuming recoding, and enable the development of more reliable and adaptable systems. Additionally, ASP may enable the creation of innovative software solutions that would otherwise be impractical due to their complexity.

This study explores a complex control issue where costs fluctuate frequently in response to random events and unexpected occurrences, and the impact of these events on the system is significant, causing the costs to change substantially. The goal is to minimize the total cost, including the immediate cost and the expected future costs caused by future random events, where the expected future costs are influenced by the probability of the next random event occurring and are thus non-linear. The key question is whether it is possible to find an optimal way to respond to random events in real-time. Because the system's response to random events can change suddenly, it is challenging to determine whether the optimal way to respond involves changing the system's response suddenly, changing it gradually, or leaving it unchanged. The solution to this issue is the focus of the study, and it requires verifying the existence of an optimal way to respond to random events in real-time.

We analyze a leptonic system that contains only one type of leptoquark, which is not commonly found in grand unified theories, using data from the Large Hadron Collider. By applying an uneven scalar-lepton coupling and assuming a significant mass difference between the two leptoquark states, we perform a thorough reinterpretation of three distinct searches. The results show that some currently unused contours in search plots can yield substantial amounts of data that could be relevant to our analysis, especially when considering the unique scenario of unequal couplings. Specifically, we find that some of these contours can provide evidence for leptoquark existence with masses around 1000 GeV in a scenario where the charged and neutral leptoquark have significantly different masses.

In educational settings, students are frequently presented with temporal sequence data that comprise brief, complex scenes from nature. These sequences often have multiple possible interpretations and require students to engage in active learning to understand their underlying patterns. Current machine learning methods are ineffective in processing these sequences due to their high-dimensional and transient nature. Existing approaches typically simplify high-dimensional data by selecting key features but often overlook the essential temporal connections. In contrast, our proposed framework combines guided learning with a hidden state model to effectively process temporal sequence data. By leveraging a feature extraction method called multivariate adaptive regression splines, it extracts relevant feature information from a high-dimensional space. We demonstrate the performance benefits of this framework in a simulated study and verify its superiority over conventional methods. Furthermore, it exhibits promising results in a real-world application, surpassing the accuracy of conventional methods in a wildlife recognition task.

Quantifying the excitation of the CI lines in molecular gas reservoirs is essential for accurately determining the physical properties and exchange rates of gas in galaxies. By comparing the observed CI emission to model predictions, we perform a statistical analysis of 321 U/LIRGs at a redshift z less than 0.04, using a large dataset from the HERA and ALMA Observations Database. Our results show that the CI lines are generally subthermal, with an average fraction of thermalized spin kinetic energy around 0.45, exhibiting no clear correlation with other key galaxy parameters, including infrared luminosity, systemic velocity, and gas velocity. However, we do observe a weak negative correlation between CI thermalization and gas mass. By considering a range of possible exchange rates and gas temperatures, we create three distinct categories of galaxies based on their CI thermalization. These findings suggest that using the ratio of CI (2-3) to CI (1-0) as an independent indicator of gas excitation may be a useful alternative to other methods.

We investigate a vectorlike compositeness scenario for top quarks and the first two generations of fermions, focusing on the impact on $K$ and $B$ anomalies through effective four-quark operators. Our analysis reveals that the model can simultaneously address the $K^+$ anomaly at 2$\sigma$ confidence and the $R_K$ anomaly in $B$ mesons at 1$\sigma$ confidence for a large range of relevant energies. Furthermore, we find that the degree of compositeness for the top quark must exceed 0.5, with a preferred value of approximately 0.8. Additionally, we discover that the preferred parameter values lead to a significant increase in the top quark decay width, which could be as high as 100% of its standard model value, potentially affecting top quark pair precision measurements.

This research focuses on solving the full series reconstruction problem for binary codes, which is a long-standing challenge in coding theory. By leveraging a recently introduced concept called "arrangements" and their corresponding "Hamming distance," researchers have divided the code into several subclasses that can be analyzed with simplified constructions. You will learn the basics of code arrangements and the associated "Hamming distance" in Part I of this study. Building on previous work by Koyama and Tavsoe, this research specifically explores the code arrangements defined by the exponential function, rectangular function, and cubic function. It demonstrates that the series reconstruction problem has a feasible solution for certain binary code arrangements, which were previously unexplored, and offers two approaches to construct these code arrangements. Furthermore, this study establishes an upper limit for the code rate of arrangements with the exponential, rectangular, and cubic functions. By achieving this advancement, the total number of code arrangements with a solvable series reconstruction problem has been significantly increased, providing a foundation for further exploration and potentially more general applications.

This research focuses on leveraging hierarchical frameworks to enhance musical instrument recognition, with an emphasis on novel instruments that have not been previously identified. Since existing datasets predominantly contain images of traditional instruments, our work relies on a unique dataset comprising images of instruments from diverse cultures, with detailed labels spanning from general categories to precise instrument names. By employing a multi-task learning approach with hierarchical representations, our experiments demonstrate that using such frameworks yields superior results compared to non-hierarchical methods, with a notable improvement in achieving high accuracy rates for identifying rare instruments. Moreover, our findings showcase the effectiveness of meta-learning strategies in efficiently adapting to new instruments within new categories.

Academic researchers often rely on systematic reviews and rigorous evaluation to inform their search for information. However, our experience searching for specific details in broad topics like AI safety, machine learning in medicine, and natural language processing was less than satisfactory. In response, we've created a comprehensive set of precise questions and comprehensive answers to serve as a starting point for further research, with each answer building upon a core research article. We believe this collection of information-seeking queries and resulting conversations represents a more effective approach to searching for information, and we're willing to share our findings with others in the information-seeking community.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting the gravitational influence of numerous supermassive black hole binaries on the motions of pulsars in the sky. In a recent study, a comprehensive understanding of PTAs' sensitivity was gained by conducting thorough simulations of elliptical binary systems' interactions with pulsars. These simulations were executed at high post-Newtonian accuracies, allowing for predictions of peculiar velocity patterns that are critical for predicting pulsar movements and, in turn, PTA signals. By comparing these detailed predictions to simpler models, scientists found the differences to be minimal, at least for pulsars located farther than 10 kpc from the Earth. Furthermore, a breakthrough was made in a line of custom-made fast Fourier transform algorithms designed to compute PTA signals efficiently. These advancements will greatly contribute to the ongoing effort to maximize PTA's potential by identifying potential pulsars suitable for alignment with ground-based detectors like LIGO.

We establish that in ASEP, a velocity process evolves from an initial configuration and is associated with a velocity measure that is a marginal distribution of the ASEP velocity process's equilibrium measure. This velocity measure is shown to be a velocity version of the speed-up/slow-down process introduced by Jansevan Rensburg and Rivin. Furthermore, we prove that the private velocity process's velocity measure is a factorizable measure that is entirely determined by the underlying space's geometry.

This study examines various mathematical frameworks used to analyze epidemic outbreaks, ultimately applying these concepts to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. As governments make critical decisions based on epidemic data, it is essential to understand the underlying models that predict disease spread. We evaluate and contrast SEIR-based models, before modeling the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic using an SEIR framework, with reference to publicly available epidemic data. Our analysis explores the effects of non-pharmaceutical interventions on disease spread, incorporating human movement dynamics into our model. Additionally, we investigate the occurrence of second waves in pandemic epidemics. Our research is under continuous development and open to collaboration.

We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on the impact of a linear external potential on the particle's Shannon entropy. Next, we derive the probabilities of finding the Majorana fermion in various energy and vortex states. Ultimately, the influence of the external potential on the Majorana fermion's statistical behavior is explored in one-dimensional space.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym recognition and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This system can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. Furthermore, the system's source code has been made available for further exploration at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent light inducing a transformation between spin-up atomic pairs and corresponding linked molecular entities. These systems, comprised of two hyperfine spin components, can be reconfigured using laser pulses that create a pathway for atom-molecule conversion. We have determined photoassociation probabilities, successful transformation probabilities, and the influence of light intensity, system size, and scattering cross-section. Furthermore, we have examined how laser coherence impacts this process and found that, under certain conditions, it can lead to molecule creation through a mechanism involving three-body recombination.

Our proposed storage system, called DNA-FS, is designed to enhance the data management capabilities of sequence-based storage through a hierarchical structure that facilitates efficient updating and querying of data. By utilizing a binary tree organization, DNA-FS significantly reduces the computational requirements for both query and update operations by at least an order of magnitude over existing solutions. Furthermore, we have developed an optimized algorithm for maintaining query performance, which includes pinpointing the most efficient storage location, combining data from different storage sites, and prioritizing data for increased query efficiency. Through our implementation and subsequent testing, we have demonstrated that DNA-FS can provide rapid query results and efficient data updates on a physical system.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the topological invariant quantities of these systems. Unfortunately, the intricate nature of electronic systems often hinders direct observation of topological features in momentum space. Conversely, quantum photon systems offer a more manageable means to study these phenomena due to the simpler and more controllable properties of light. Recent advancements incorporate metamaterials with negative refractive index into quantum photon systems, enhancing their topological capabilities and enabling straightforward visualization of momentum-space topological structures through light flux surfaces. This article reviews the integration of negative-index metamaterials into topological quantum photon systems, highlighting the advantages these systems offer for studying topological phenomena and suggesting the potential for applying similar concepts to other fields involving wave propagation.

A complex medical issue such as brain tumor detection calls for the integration of multiple imaging modalities and sophisticated deep learning techniques. Based on 3D MRI scans, this study combines a multi-task, directionally-focused network with a dataset-driven approach to identify and classify brain tumors. The proposed MRI-based model utilizes a multi-task, directionally-focused encoder-decoder network to extract tumor-specific features from various directional views, while utilizing a dataset-driven method to predict tumor types through feature selection. By concurrently executing both classification and segmentation tasks, the multi-task network enhances accuracy and addresses potential alignment issues between tumor masks and actual growths. Experimental results on the BrainTumour13 dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, achieving better segmentation precision and a more accurate tumor classification method with a minimal number of annotations.

Computer vision problems such as reconstruction, tracking, and scene inference often rely on differentiable rendering methods to integrate visual observations and estimate physical properties or scene configurations. However, traditional rendering techniques, like photometric rendering, photon mapping, and volumetric rendering, compromise differentiability for efficiency. This compromise hinders the application of contemporary optimization techniques that leverage differentiability for robust and efficient solutions. To address this limitation, we introduce an unconventional shadow evaluation approach that maintains differentiability while mimicking the behavior of biased algorithms. By leveraging our approach, various inverse problems that involve rendering, such as shape, material, and light source estimation, can be formulated as stable and efficient problems. We illustrate the effectiveness of our method by achieving state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets for inverse problems involving multi-view images.

A popular technique, widely used for enhancing video playback on television and recording, is interlacing. This technique doubles the perceived frame rate without boosting the bandwidth, yet generates undesirable effects like visual distortion and flicker during playback. Present methods fail to balance necessary processing speed and impressive outcomes. They either miss the real-time processing requirement or yield unsatisfactory results. This study proposes an innovative approach, happening in each instant, for deep video decomposition. Leveraging convolutional neural networks, this technique achieves highly accurate results while fulfilling the strict requirement of real-time processing. Experimental data, obtained from various challenging datasets, demonstrate the method's capability to produce highly precise outcomes. Moreover, it outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in processing speed.

This paper investigates the characteristics of the neutron distribution in semi-empirical models, focusing on the relativistic and non-relativistic versions of the average field models. We calculated the square radius of the neutron distribution, an interesting quantity that isn't directly provided by the AFDM1 and AFDM3 formulas. By analyzing the results, we found that the distinction between relativistic and non-relativistic interpretations has a negligible effect on this quantity. Furthermore, our findings align with theoretical predictions, and we demonstrate that the neutron distribution properties depend primarily on the average field's characteristics rather than its relativistic or non-relativistic form.

Precise and timely flood prediction is crucial for saving lives and minimizing economic losses, which motivates the development of efficient numerical solutions for the shallow water equations (SWEs). Despite recent advances in computational technology, solving the SWEs remains challenging due to the need for high-performance linear solvers in implicit techniques, which can be time-consuming and limit the development of practical flood prediction models. Recent studies have explored the potential of deep learning to accelerate linear solvers, but such models are often limited to specific system sizes and have not been widely tested against traditional methods. This study introduces a deep learning-based solver (DLS) that can solve the shallow water equations for any initial condition and domain size, and be compared to traditional solvers such as CHOMA. The research demonstrates that the DLS can provide a 10-100 times speed-up over CHOMA, and is particularly effective in modeling complex river flows with high water depths. However, its performance declines in cases with low water depths, which suggests that further optimization is needed to make the DLS a universally reliable alternative to traditional solvers.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels
to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This research presents a
technique for automatically determining optimal exposure settings for mobile devices
and fusing images to produce HDR effects. Initially, an algorithm is proposed to
accurately detect edges and estimate luminosity levels across photos, paving the way
for selective fusion. Subsequent techniques are then outlined to refine fusion
weights, normalize luminosity disparities, and integrate photos using a weighted
average method. Prototype implementations on smartphones demonstrate the
feasibility of these techniques, with outstanding results showcased in the included
section on performance evaluation. Findings indicate that naturally lit scenes
yield exceptional HDR effects, while artificially lit scenes may require adjustments
to achieve optimal results. Key advantages of the proposed technique include
cost-effectiveness (no additional hardware required), simplicity (minimal
computational needs), and versatility (applicable to various mobile devices).

Causal machine learning models, particularly causal neural networks, are emerging with the ability to tackle complex, underlying causal structures in data. Although they show great promise, assessing the validity of inferences made by these models is extremely challenging due to the lack of knowledge about their intrinsic workings. Current analysis methods are largely restricted to basic, linear scenarios or are unsuitable for real-world applications. In contrast, our novel framework is capable of analyzing the causal architecture of any given neural network, regardless of non-linearity or the absence of explicit causal symptoms in the input data. This allows us to provide the first formal guarantees for causal neural networks in non-linear scenarios, paving the way for rigorous theoretical foundations and enhancing our understanding of the relationship between neural networks and causal models.

Achieving uniform heating within gas-solid beds is crucial for maximizing the efficiency of thermal processes, but however, temperature distributions within these systems are often non-uniform due to varying particle densities and the presence of hot spots. The inherent dynamics of gas-solid flows then further exacerbate this issue by introducing unsteady temperature distributions. The challenge of addressing this problem lies in its complexity, stemming from the need to simultaneously measure key parameters including flow velocity, particle density, and temperature distribution. The recent development of advanced computer algorithms has facilitated more precise measurements, albeit primarily for simplified flow configurations. The present study employs a cutting-edge imaging technique to directly measure temperature distributions within gas-solid beds, demonstrating its potential for mapping three-dimensional temperature profiles. The novel approach combines magnetic resonance imaging with time-domain optical imaging to determine the energy distribution within these systems. The study probes the heating dynamics of monodisperse sand flows for various flow rates and reveals distinct three-dimensional temperature profiles, featuring axial gradients in both the center and peripheral regions, along with a distinctive temperature dip in the middle of the bed. The findings also indicate that increasing the flow rate results in more pronounced temperature differences and distinct temperature layers. The study demonstrates the technique's capability to measure the effects of changing flow rate on temperature distributions.

This note represents a feeble version of the b-principle, which translates to a tangency scenario known as the Mumford line. Given a linear subspace within a Euclidean space, we seek a linear transformation that maps this subspace to a tangent space of a sphere. This objective is achievable if the dimension of the subspace exceeds one.

In large-scale computational models of cardiac mechanics, such as those based on structured and unstructured electrical activity models, the cost of computing the Jacobian matrix for these systems becomes prohibitively expensive due to the extensive cell integration required. As a result, direct solution methods are impractical, making it necessary to employ iterative solvers such as GMRES. As the dimensionality of the problem increases, the storage needs for incomplete factorization-based solvers become too demanding for current high-performance computing systems. Consequently, there is a growing interest in alternative scalable methods for determining the spectral condition number, such as estimating it from the residual growth of GMRES. While such approximations have been compared in past studies, these comparisons were made on a limited basis, focusing either on simple model problems or specific applications like cardiac mechanics. This study compares the spectral behavior of cardiac mechanics problems using both realistic tissue models and their related single-cell electrophysiology, with a particular emphasis on how these problems scale with different system sizes. We also examine how the condition number estimates from GMRES residuals hold up in practice and consider their implications for choosing appropriate solver parameters in cardiac mechanics applications.

Independent component analysis (ICA) is tested for a special type of random matrix called the "diagonalizable source matrix". This test involves generating synthetic data using the independent component analysis model and verifying that the estimated ICA model meets certain criteria. Initially, it is demonstrated that when the source matrix has distinct, real, and non-overlapping eigenvalues, it is possible to accurately recover the underlying source signals. However, when the source matrix has repeated, real, or complex eigenvalues, it is shown that it is impossible to accurately recover the underlying source signals under certain conditions. This limitation is addressed by introducing a new condition called "non-crossing partitionability", which enables accurate recovery of source signals in cases where traditional ICA methods fail.

Convincing video generation, combining animation with live footage to create a realistic video, has gained significant interest in recent years due to its numerous potential applications, such as video editing and virtual event production. Leveraging AI technology, particularly deep learning algorithms, has become the norm for achieving this level of video manipulation. Currently, there is a lack of comprehensive documentation covering this topic, prompting us to create a detailed survey on convincing video generation, including various techniques, evaluation metrics, and associated tools. Our work is expected to provide a valuable reference for researchers and developers looking to contribute to this field and create practical applications using this technology.

The concept of safety zones around vessels has long been recognized, with the idea that these areas protect both the vessel and nearby swimmers. However, recent research suggests that this perception of safety may be illusory, with risks present even within these designated areas. This study aims to extend the existing body of knowledge by investigating how swimmers' understanding of safety zones evolves in response to deceptive feedback. A simulated swimming environment was used to explore this outcome, with the results showing that deceptive feedback can lead swimmers to adjust their perceptions of safety zones, with implications for the development of effective safety protocols.

Recently, acoustic metagratings have gained significant attention for their potential to seamlessly integrate with integrated circuit systems and enable precise wavelength-scale manipulation of sound. However, the lack of efficient and precise mass fabrication methods has limited their production, especially at the ultra-high wavelength scale. Advances in two-photon polymerization have enabled the precise creation of complex acoustic structures, but their scalability and mass-producibility in this technique require further improvement. This study introduces a novel method using two-photon polymerization that combines with electron beam writing to fabricate acoustic metagratings at the nano-scale, overcoming previous limitations of bulk production. The technique involves using the two-photon polymerization method to create micro-scale periodic structures that operate as high-efficiency acoustic transmission gratings, while the electron beam writer precisely constructs the sub-wavelength unit cell at the interface between two periodic structures. This hybrid method allows for the mass production of acoustic metagratings with refined features, and our research demonstrates that the fabricated devices exhibit over 90% transmission efficiency with a small loss angle. Moreover, we demonstrate a micro-acoustic lens made from a metagrating that showcases a focusing depth ratio of around 50, outperforming conventional damping-filled lenses. This breakthrough in mass production of acoustic metagratings using two-photon polymerization has vast applications, from acoustic energy manipulation to sensing and medical treatments.

We examine the long-term diffusion behavior in a diverse range of random permeability configurations across different dimensions. By defining a relative position in the permeability field as $\Delta\log\theta(\mathbf{x})$, we investigate its statistical properties in order to understand how they influence the overall diffusion behavior. Our results indicate that the observed non-Gaussian anomalies can arise from moderate variations in the permeability field and demonstrate this through specific examples in two and three-dimensional spaces. Furthermore, we find that the dispersion measure, derived from the second moment of the relative position, is a more detailed indicator of diffusion behavior than the standard mean squared displacement. Additionally, we show that the non-Gaussian characteristics of the relative position can be quantified using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, which facilitates the comparison of numerical models with corresponding theoretical models of diffusion.

This paper provides an in-depth examination of linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between optical resonators and waveguides. We demonstrate that in an arbitrary resonator or waveguide, Kerr nonlinearity leads to a scalar chi(3) effect, whereas linear interactions result in both scalar and cross-coupling effects. To fully characterize the behavior of coupled systems, we analyze both individual components and the interaction between them. For resonators with identical linear and Kerr properties, we observe symmetric mode patterns, whereas asymmetry leads to the activation of previously inaccessible modes. In waveguides, mode patterns are determined by Kerr nonlocality. When two resonators or waveguides are Kerr identical, coupling occurs through an optical mode. However, when Kerr properties differ, coupling occurs through both optical modes and converted modes. If the linear and Kerr properties of two components are asymmetrical, coupling can occur through multiple optical modes, and we identify critical conditions for this multi-mode coupling. These findings have far-reaching implications for the design of optical communication systems, enabling the selection of systems based on desired multi-mode coupling, and potentially leading to the development of optical transistors.

This paper introduces a novel approach to a well-known control theorem, focusing on the convergence of continuous filters in the context of control systems driven by noise. By relaxing certain assumptions, particularly those related to the boundedness of control inputs, we establish a converse theorem for the strong convergence of internal and external filters. Notably, our conditions are less restrictive than those required for the classical converse theorem. Building upon this result, we also develop a converse linearization approach, facilitating the achievement of almost sure convergence and providing a specific control strategy to do so. Key aspects of our findings involve the utilization of a discrete time framework and the use of the Feller-Tonelli theorem.

A novel deep learning framework is proposed, consisting of a generative adversarial network (GAN), to significantly enhance turbulent flow visualization at high Reynolds numbers, beyond the capabilities of direct numerical simulation (DNS). The GAN is designed to generate highly detailed, realistic turbulent velocity fields from limited-resolution data obtained at high Reynolds numbers. Through training with low-resolution DNS data at different Reynolds numbers, the network demonstrates its ability to create accurate, high-resolution velocity fields, even in cases where the DNS is unfeasible due to high computational costs associated with high Reynolds numbers. The results show that this deep learning approach can successfully produce turbulent velocity fields at very high Reynolds numbers (up to 40,000) using low-resolution DNS at lower Reynolds numbers (up to 5,600). These findings have important implications for the development of turbulent flow visualization techniques and suggest potential applications in enhanced flow visualization and realism in virtual reality applications.

This note presents an interpretation of the wave equation as a means of describing particle behavior, differing from classical mechanics. In quantum physics, particles exhibit both wave-like and particle-like characteristics. The wave equation is central to this theory and forms the basis for many approximations and models in physics. Various solutions to the wave equation have been found over time, often corresponding to specific physical scenarios, such as one-dimensional scenarios, scattering phenomena, and confined spaces. These solutions display interesting patterns, such as superposition, interference, and tunneling. The note aims to provide an intuitive understanding of the wave equation and its significance within quantum physics.

In the open-world scenario, systems must adapt to continuously emerging new information, requiring a dynamic approach to dealing with uncertainties. The proposed Energy-Driven Open-World Uncertainty Framework addresses this challenge by utilizing an energy-based method to continuously assess uncertainties based on the system's understanding of its environment. The framework involves two key components. Firstly, the Specification Language for Assurances is used to express uncertainties as reachability problems in a changing environment. Secondly, the energy-based uncertainty quantification calculates a critical value that indicates the likelihood of a specific outcome occurring within a certain time frame. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a case study involving a self-driving car. The study shows that traditional methods fail to account for uncertainties in an increasingly complex environment, ultimately resulting in conservative estimates that do not accurately reflect the system's ability to operate safely. In contrast, the energy-based method provides a more accurate assessment of uncertainties, enabling the development of reliable assurance cases in an open-world scenario.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models typically struggle when faced with new tasks beyond their training data, as they often become sidetracked by previously learned information. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks that can test continual learning performance across multiple tasks. These frameworks enable the comprehensive study of key factors influencing continual learning, such as the recall penalty and episode length, on complex problems involving multiple tasks, particularly in scenarios where rewards are sparse. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge environment that allows for flexible evaluation of continual learning strategies in rich, 3D worlds, and we highlight the significant benefits of using this environment through rigorous experiments highlighting the importance of careful framework design and the value of using exogenous hints to accelerate learning.

We introduce a novel, declarative process framework that leverages streams for supervision and exploration, addressing real-world challenges posed by ever-changing processes. These processes often involve complex, interdependent tasks that require significant time to complete, necessitating periodic task re-evaluation and frequent process variations. Our approach is designed to provide optimal solutions for these processes, taking into consideration their dynamic nature. To achieve this, we develop a flexible, declarative representation that can efficiently handle flowing data and varying process conditions. This representation allows us to integrate explicit exploration goals into our framework, ensuring that the process makes informed decisions about which data to prioritize. Our approach includes a robust, declarative language that can handle real-world process instances, as well as a versatile stream management system that can adapt to changing process definitions and optimize data processing. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms conventional methods by processing tasks more efficiently and effectively, regardless of the size of the dataset.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden transition from localization to non-localization. Our theory and experimental results indicate that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light localization can transition back to non-localization at higher quasiperiodic modulation strengths for some states, representing an unusual phenomenon. Additionally, this occurrence can be understood through a mathematical model that represents dimerized interactions over extended distances.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Data Processing System (DPS) to regulate its operation, reconfigure its optics, and fine-tune its performance based on real-time data. The DPS will be responsible for converting raw data into usable science output for Liger's sensitive spectral data. To accomplish this, the DPS will apply established data transformation techniques and unique Liger-specific algorithms. The development of the DPS involved creating a comprehensive software framework, which will serve as an open resource for the astronomical community. The framework comprises a diverse range of components, including a complex system for managing and prioritizing data, as well as specialized tools for configuring the devices and tracing data pathways. Furthermore, the community can leverage the framework's modular design to adapt its components for other similar applications.

A novel approach is proposed to enhance the super-resolution limit in bi-photon spatial mode demultiplexing, surpassing the standard quantum limit. This method involves introducing an entanglement between the photons' polarizations, leveraged through the Malus distribution following partial projective measurements. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this strategy can yield a $1.4\tilde{r}$ improvement in super-resolution, with $\tilde{r}$ representing the ratio of resolving power to that of a single photon. Furthermore, this approach is shown to be compatible with the formation angle increase issue, enabling demonstration of the method with modified optical systems.
This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties.

In dynamic ecological systems with multiple timescales, population counts on longer timescales often fluctuate significantly, reflecting the internal dynamics of the system, while shorter timescales reveal the influence of external factors and internal processes generating variability. This study navigates these variations to uncover early signs and reduced-dimensional representations of substantial population shifts in North Atlantic right whales. Initially, our analysis separates the longer timescales from the shorter-term variability and identifies the governing equations for the longer-time fluctuations. Next, we create a data-driven model capturing the intrinsic variability of the system and an external forcing component. This reduced-dimensional model highlights the importance of prey distribution, body condition, and recorded whale deaths in relation to observed data. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the importance of preconditioning data to eliminate the influence of the longer-time fluctuations and identify key features in the data. Finally, our results show that combined features of the data, including prey distribution, body condition, and recorded whale deaths, serve as sufficient early indicators for significant population shifts.

The observed relationship between star formation rates and gas fractions, a behavior that changes at the high mass end for galaxies, is not well understood. Unfortunately, the existing observations are limited, making it difficult to study this relationship in massive star-forming galaxies. To better comprehend the similarity between these galaxies and the broader population of galaxies, we need a larger, more diverse dataset. Using the MASCOT-S2 galaxy sample which includes 767 near-infrared selected galaxies observed with MASSIVEL for a total of 1786 spectra, we were able to determine the gas fractions for all of the galaxies through both optical and infrared methods. Our measurements show a distinct break in the star formation rate versus gas fraction relationship, similar to previous findings, and confirmed that it occurs at a sequence-specific mass. Our analysis distinguishes between disk and bulge components and reveals that the relationship holds true for disk sections but not for bulge sections. Furthermore, our research indicates that bulges have a higher mass-to-light ratio than the rest of the galaxy, a finding that aligns with previous studies. When accounting for the mass of stars in bulges, our results show that the relationship breaks down at a star formation rate 10 times higher than when only considering the disk's star formation rate. This implies that massive star-forming galaxies have a large bulge and once this effect is taken into consideration, their overall morphology is similar to that of less massive galaxies.

Sentiment analysis across languages has proven to be more complicated than
for a single language due to differing writing styles, extensive vocabularies
and poor labelled data. This study proposes a multi-task learning approach,
utilizing limited labelled data for sentiment analysis in several languages
and a vast amount of unlabeled data for other tasks. The proposed model
achieves superior results on six diverse language datasets for sentiment
analysis, outperforming current state-of-the-art models that rely on
sentiment-specific pretraining. Our model also successfully extends to
low-resource languages such as Nepali, achieving 10% better accuracy on the
Nepali Sentiment Treebank dataset in comparison to baseline models.

We're addressing the challenge of maintaining accuracy in distributed databases, specifically in scenarios where data is updated frequently and efficiently required. Our research focuses on a fundamental problem: achieving consistency within an updatable cache by validating cache lines and generating notifications for conflicts. We're presenting two novel techniques to accelerate performance: a self-invalidating mechanism for reducing unnecessary revalidation, and a self-devaluation approach to minimize notification latency. Our model incorporates a cache hierarchy, where only the bottom-level cache can interact directly with the database, and all communication with upper caches occurs via data accessed during execution. Our analysis shows that both techniques yield a 2-fold improvement in performance, and integrating them results in optimal performance with a 4-fold better performance than traditional approaches in scenarios with high conflict rates.
Freiman's 3k-4 theorem is expanded upon in this essay, with multiple independent proofs presented.

Consider a fractional Brownian motion (fBm) B^H in R^d, with Hurst index H in (0,1), and its version B^H_s with a time-change using a non-decreasing, continuous function \phi. We examine the measure of the set of paths from B^H_{\phi(t)} for almost all fBm realizations, and express this measure in terms of the dimension of its interior. Subsequent to some initial results, we focus primarily on the case when d equals 1. We demonstrate that the expected measure of the set's interior is positive when the fBm's drift parameter satisfies a specific inequality, and that this occurs more frequently as H approaches 1. Conversely, the set's interior has zero measure for all H in (0,1). We also investigate the scenario where the fBm's drift parameter exceeds a certain threshold, and establish that the set's interior has a non-empty interior with a measure proportional to (1-H)^{(1+2(1-H))/2}, given certain conditions.

This research employs Dirac's variational principle, in conjunction with the Jackiw-Kerman function, to investigate the H\'enon-Heiles potential. By utilizing a simple wave function with cluster properties, centered around the ground state, we calculate the energy minimization to obtain an estimate for the ground state energy. The approach is validated through comparisons with existing results for solvable models, and numerical calculations are carried out to determine the rotational vibration energy for different H\'enon-Heiles configurations.

X-ray images of COVID-19 patients contain underlying information that can forecast their critical care unit (ICU) admission odds. This study aims to examine the connection between these images and the probability of ICU admission. Initially, a comprehensive dataset that includes chest X-ray images and corresponding healthcare records for 1378 COVID-19 patients was thoroughly reviewed. Subsequent investigations employed a variety of advanced techniques to analyze this data, revealing distinct patterns in X-ray images that correlate with the likelihood of ICU admission. Notably, three distinct features were found: (1) alveolar fragmentation, (2) cardiac enlargement, and (3) pulmonary pleura involvement. When integrated with existing COVID-19 classification features, these findings can enhance the prediction of ICU admission with a notable improvement in accuracy.

Let's consider a simplicial space X and a simplicial map p: X -> K representing a simplical simplicial set K. The global simplicial bundle defined by M. Grandis and R. Parzano in [6] consists of the simplicial space X times K, denoted by M, with the projection defined by the simplicial map p to K. We demonstrate that M admits a simplicial group structure when K is a simplicial simplicial set with a connected simplicial fundamental group.

One Severe Flaw in Visual Relationship Detection: The Erroneous Positive Problem and Its Impact is Investigated in this work.  We first pinpoint the source of the problem by analyzing how incorrect relationships arise from misleading object categories.  Then, a 2-Stage approach is proposed to counter this effect, where the initial stage filters out potentially erroneous pairs based on a contextless classification, followed by a re-identification of genuine pairs within the narrowed down group using a more accurate comparison method.  The effectiveness of this approach is consistently verified across multiple datasets and evaluation metrics.  Moreover, our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in various tests.

The delta sampling framework was proposed in 2019, offering a supervised learning approach for action recognition. This method involves creating a dataset with labeled data, where samples are selected based on their central position in a temporal sequence. However, the performance of this framework is hindered by limited data and poor image quality issues. To address these challenges, this research modifies the delta sampling framework by integrating R-BERT, a pre-trained language model, and introduces two innovative sampling techniques. The proposed framework is evaluated on the CMU motion dataset under low-light conditions and demonstrates enhanced performance compared to the original delta sampling framework.

Modern convolutional neural networks achieve exceptional accuracy but at the cost of intricate architecture complexity, rendering traditional direct programming approaches ineffective. In an effort to enhance processing efficiency, a novel method has been proposed by combining the concepts of data parallelism and spatially distributed processing through multiple concurrent processors. This technique has been implemented using an addressable memory framework on a FPGA, where each processing element is connected to a small neighborhood of memory addresses. The resulting system exhibits high data locality, minimal data transfer, and optimized memory usage. With a relatively small number of addressable memory locations, the network can be processed at a rate of 19.03 fps for video input, outperforming a base CPU-based implementation by a factor of 30.3 while achieving a 2.5 times increase in frame rate with the same CPU.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three young galaxy clusters at z ~ 3, and observed that galaxies in these clusters have significantly different physical characteristics compared to those in lower-redshift galaxy clusters. These high-z galaxy clusters have smaller, more compact galaxy populations with features similar to those found in recently discovered galaxy populations in the early universe. In contrast, galaxies in these clusters have larger, more disordered bulges and are often lopsided, with 20% exhibiting disordered stellar distributions and 10% showing signs of tidal interactions.
