A recent model excelled in extracting social determinants by understanding the entire record's meaning but relied on specialized clinical knowledge. In contrast, our proposed framework leverages a different type of knowledge called "markers" to facilitate the automatic extraction of social determinants from clinical notes.Markers comprise predefined pairs of a concept and its associated cue, which can originate from various sources, including medical texts, ontologies, and existing knowledge bases. When applying the framework to clinical notes, it employs a combination of both zero-shot and shot-based classification to identify relevant social determinants by detecting the corresponding markers. In experiments conducted for three diverse social determinants – Housing, Transportation, and Food insecurity – our framework demonstrated superior performance, outperforming existing state-of-the-art models by achieving a 12% increase in F1 score.

This study is centered on a model describing the rhythmic swimming movement of a scallop, which can switch between two opposing jet velocities to achieve forward and reverse locomotion. We examine three primary configurations: when the body and the jet are aligned with the water's surface, when the body is perpendicular to the water's surface, and when there's an angular displacement between the body and the jet. For each scenario, we use Pontryagin's Maximum Principle to identify the optimal jet velocity profile. Nonetheless, obtaining analytical solutions proves challenging; hence, we focus on numerical solutions instead. When the body and the jet are aligned, we employ linearization to derive an approach for determining optimal trajectories. In the other scenarios, we use the optimal solution in the first configuration as a basis and observe that the optimal velocity outside of this initial range is divided into two distinct components. We also investigate how changing the water's resistance or the scallop's mass affects the optimal movement in the aligned body-jet configuration.

The COVID-19 pandemic led to significant changes in human behavior worldwide as governments enforced strict social distancing measures to slow pandemic spread. Researchers studied mobile phone data from a large, diverse population in a capital city (Mexico City) to examine changes in urban interaction patterns and their connection to income levels. Analyzing three key indicators - location visit frequency within the city, diversity of visited locations, and time spent in public places - they discovered a notable shift in users' behavior during the pandemic. Although all populations initially reduced urban interaction, as time went on, lower-income individuals returned to their normal city interaction patterns while higher-income individuals maintained their lowered frequency. As a result, the gap between these behaviorally shifting populations grew, ultimately reflecting the increased disparities evident throughout the pandemic's second year.

The formation of massive stars is subject to a longstanding mystery: how are massive young objects accumulated or merged without disruption to form massive stars?  It is commonly accepted that massive stars require a significant mass accumulation in a short period of time.  While previous research has primarily focused on protostar-mass spectra, our analysis takes a unique approach, using computational modeling to track the growth of massive protostars and surrounding disks within a high-density molecular core.  This method allows for a more realistic representation of grain growth, evaporation of particles, and viscous disk development.  Through this process, we observe that in optimal environments, the disk can supply up to 10 times the protostar's mass, with an average of 5-6 times the protostar's mass.  However, in cases where the disk breaks apart due to gravitational forces, it can still contribute 2-3 times the protostar's mass.  Furthermore, our findings indicate that in approximately 20-30% of ideal conditions, two massive protostars can merge into a single star with a mass equivalent to or greater than 10 M_.  This research offers a more comprehensive understanding of massive star formation, emphasizing the potential role of protostar mergers in the development of massive stars.

Buchholz and others established the principles of wedge-locality and net coherence as fundamental characteristics of physical networks of observables. We examine how these principles restrict the algebraic structure of physical systems by analyzing their interplay with the Longo-Witten endomorphisms, which serve as a universal tool for creating local and semi-local algebras within a network of observables. Specifically, we demonstrate that any physical network of observables must be compatible with the cone-local and network-coherent endomorphisms, and that these restrictions significantly narrow the possible spectrum of physical systems. Moreover, we find that the category of wedge-local networks of observables is fully determined by the cone-local and network-coherent endomorphisms, and that it encompasses both the chiral and non-chiral physical systems. Furthermore, we prove that the category of physical networks of observables is conservative, meaning that any wedge-local network of observables can be obtained from the cone-local and network-coherent endomorphisms, and that it is closed under the auto-duality transformation. Additionally, we identify a vast class of physical systems that correspond to wedge-local networks of observables with semi-local interconnections.

Recent studies claiming a significant increase in pediatric cancer near 5G cell towers are unfounded. To verify this finding, we re-analyzed the original data presented in Kruglikov and Johansson's research. Furthermore, we addressed the methodological limitations of that study and developed a quantitative assessment of 5G radiation exposure. Our calculation shows that in the scenarios examined, the predicted radiation levels fall below the measurable threshold. Given the very small amounts of radiation involved, it is likely that even the most sensitive measurements would struggle to detect a difference in cancer incidence rates as low as 10%. Our analysis suggests that in order to accurately assess the health impacts of 5G radiation, much larger datasets would be required in order for significant statistical trends to emerge. Ultimately, we believe that before publishing such research, authors should provide the technical details of their analysis, especially when it involves scientific concepts like electromagnetic fields and the physical properties of cells and humans.

This research focuses on modulated long-wave train existence within a two-dimensional, incompressible flow that includes uniform vorticity, and it proves that a Hamiltonian-formulated Dysthe equation represents the leading order of the problem's solution.

This paper proposes a differential framework for integrating over convex domains in real-variable analysis. We establish a Stokes theorem for forms that are integrable over these domains, using a differential approach. To do this, we first demonstrate the relationship between this approach and the traditional one involving differential forms. Next, we show that the differential approach can be applied to a broad class of convex domains, including those with non-closed boundaries. Finally, we introduce an operation analogous to de Rham cohomology and demonstrate its relationship to harmonic forms within these domains.

Our proposed framework uses a layered navigation approach, fueled by sonar data, to achieve goal-oriented behavior in underwater environments. This algorithmic method leverages a goal state representation and prioritized decision-making to optimize its operations for efficiency. To overcome computational challenges in real-time underwater goal finding, we have implemented a novel method, blending sonar data to reduce processing demands. By simplifying sensor readings and combining them, this technique enhances navigation performance by minimizing distractions and improving filtering results. We have tested our model using the Navy Sonar Data Set, a vast and complex dataset representing real-world underwater conditions, and our results show that it outperforms existing navigation methods. Due to its layered design, our approach is also easily adaptable to various underwater sensors and environments.

The issue of fake news has become increasingly prominent in recent years, necessitating the development of efficient methods for detecting false information on the internet. Current techniques typically focus on analyzing verified news pairs to train artificial intelligence models, which can then identify false news by predicting previously labeled information. In contrast, our novel approach leverages advanced text summarization capabilities to differentiate false from true news. For each piece of false news, multiple distinct false news articles are used to generate separate summary descriptions, which are then employed to create a comprehensive summary covering all false details. Conversely, a single accurate news article's summary is utilized as a comparison. Our experimental results demonstrate that this technique achieves superior performance when compared to conventional learning-based methods.

This research investigates how the characteristics of a Gaussian random field change when it is subjected to a linear transformation, with a specific focus on the effects of bending and its impact on the upper tail of the field's distribution. Although the transformation has an evident impact, our findings show that it does not significantly alter many of the field's features. In contrast, we discover that the upper tail of a normally distributed random field is highly susceptible to the type of transformation and can be controlled through the specification of mean and variance parameters. Consequently, we propose modifying the Morschadtl transformation to account for Gaussian random fields undergoing bending. This revised transformation retains the original form but with an added parameter that is utilized in the analysis of such fields' upper tails.

This research targets addressing security concerns in Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA) networks by applying quantum cryptography. Specifically, a quantum code named Peres-Mermin box (PMB) is proposed to safeguard information transmission between a central controller and quantum users sharing the same unlicensed frequency band. The code's functionality is then demonstrated in a scenario where users employ NOMA to receive encoded signals, and an unauthorized user launches an attack. Our results show that the proposed code can prevent unauthorized access and ensure reliable communication in the presence of noise, thus providing a foundation for the development of quantum secure NOMA networks. Furthermore, our study assumes that a pre-agreed classical code has already been implemented to address issues such as synchronization and phase error correction.

When dealing with noisy data that isn't perfectly aligned, traditional PCA methods based on $\ell_2$-norm optimization can be inadequate, often leading to undesirable results due to their sensitivity to rotation. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces a rotationally invariant PCA formulation based on $\ell_1$-norm optimization and develops an efficient, linearly convergent algorithm to solve it. The algorithm combines elements of the FISTA and NESTA frameworks, taking advantage of proximal mapping techniques to tackle each coordinate separately. Moreover, the paper proves that using an approximate proximal map leads to a uniformly linearly convergent solution. To demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness, several numerical experiments are included, showing it outperforms both traditional PCA and a non-rotationally invariant $\ell_1$-norm PCA method based on the augmented Lagrangian framework.

Recently, pre-trained language models like BERT have significantly improved question answering models, demonstrating the ability to successfully complete semantic annotation tasks. Building upon this success, our research focuses on revising the semantic annotations generated by BERT, which are utilized in question answering datasets, particularly those related to emotions. We establish a BERT-enhanced revision framework, incorporating active learning and few-shot learning techniques to enhance performance. Notably, our approach shows improved results over BERT-only revision, according to experimental data.

We investigate a variant of partial-order partial-game in which all elements are comparably ordered, and our primary objective is to demonstrate that this variant possesses greater complexity than its scalar counterpart, when played with two players who compete. Additionally, we establish a connection between this variant and a specific type of partial game that is symmetric in nature. Furthermore, within a broader theoretical framework known as modal logic, we draw parallels between the concept of epistemic possibility and the strategy required to win at totally ordered partial-game, before finally proving that the game in question shares many similarities with a fundamental concept within the realm of modal logic, specifically transitivity.

The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding of its primary distinguishing feature - the discrepancy in white dwarf spin and orbital periods. To gain insight into this phenomenon, a thorough analysis of X-ray spectral data was conducted on both asynchronous and normal polars using XMM-Newton observations. The study compares the X-ray hardness of both categories and reveals that hard X-ray spectra are predominantly found in asynchronous polars. No correlation was discovered between X-ray hardness and orbital or white dwarf spin periods in either category. However, a link was established between X-ray hardness and the accretion spot coverage in asynchronous polars, suggesting that covered hot spots could contribute significantly to the enhanced hard X-ray spectra observed in this subtype.

This project's primary goal is to discuss how a unified and a partitioned Reduced Basis Method can address Fluid-Structure Interaction problems, focusing particularly on problems involving nonlinear fluid dynamics and multiple linear solid mechanics systems.

For over two decades, researchers have been investigating a fundamental query affecting mobile robots: given their surroundings, can they generate a map of their environment, and if so, what map format works best?  In response to rising demands for visual map creation methods, a range of representations have emerged, from simple graph models to complex layouts, but often lacking are evaluations that assess these models' practical applications.  In a breakthrough, researchers have developed HiTMap, a novel, flexible, and easily-implementable evaluation framework that assesses the navigational capabilities of different map representations in unknown settings.  Through extensive testing, they have demonstrated the effectiveness of their approach by conducting robustness, generalization, planning, and real-world navigation assessments of various map formats, including popular choices like Grid, Triangle, Delaunay, and Voronoi models.  In their study, they have discovered that simple, easily-generated representations can excel over more complex alternatives in real-world navigation applications.  In addition to advancing HiTMap maps through their proposed evaluation framework, they have also introduced an innovative biologically-inspired method for creating high-quality HiTMap maps suitable for a range of applications.  In conclusion, their groundbreaking research has paved the way for the development of high-quality, practical navigation maps, and their evaluation framework is sure to guide future studies in this exciting field.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval Aggressive Detection Task is the subject of this paper. Our approach to identifying aggressive tweets on social media was presented at SemEval 2019, where we achieved a high-ranking performance in the ranking subgroup. Our team's leadership shifted from the previous year, and through analysis of ranking and classification approaches, we determined that BERT's basic architecture was the top-performing model. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that BERT's reliance on pre-trained data may result in biased classifications. In the classification segment, our team's simple yet effective approach using linear support vector machines and feature selection resulted in a high-ranking performance among 137 submissions.

The precise measurement of local magnetic fields is essential for studying various phenomena, including atomic and particle physics, as well as biological and medical applications. Currently, atomic interferometry offers one of the most accurate methods for this measurement. However, achieving sensitive measurements in atomic interferometry experiments is impeded by magnetic noise originating from the atomic sample itself, which can arise due to various sources such as imperfect polarization or maladjusted optical components. Overcoming this challenge requires a noise-free atomic sample that only interacts with a minimal amount of external magnetic field. This can be achieved by utilizing superconducting materials that exhibit the Meissner effect, which forces the external magnetic field into a thin layer close to the surface. By incorporating a superconducting film into an atomic interferometry setup, we demonstrate a significant reduction of magnetic noise by approximately 100 times. This involves a detailed explanation of how this setup functions, as well as the theoretical foundation for achieving precise measurements of local magnetic fields. Furthermore, we outline potential approaches to further optimize this setup, which could result in a 10-fold improvement in sensitivity.

We investigate the interplay between spin and heat in monolayer MoSe2, MoS2, WS2, and WSe2 using the first-principles calculations. Our analysis reveals that changing the chemical potential has a significant effect on the thermal conductivity and carrier density near the K point in these materials. By examining the thermal conductivity, carrier density, and magnetic moment across the band gap, we identify critical values of chemical potential that mark the transition from high to low thermal conductivity and from small to large magnetic moment. These transitions are accompanied by a significant change in the carrier density. Furthermore, we demonstrate that applying a magnetic field can modulate the thermal conductivity and magnetic moment by controlling the orbital coupling. Our theoretical framework is applicable to other 2D semiconductors, and our results suggest that the magnetic properties of these materials can be evaluated through thermal transport measurements.

We investigate how electron-electron and electron-photon interactions influence the behavior of gap-plasmons. Our analysis considers a two-dimensional system with a varying gap width, ranging from infinitesimally small to several nanometers. The electron-electron interaction is examined in the context of both a semi-parabolic and an exact density-functional theory calculation, while the electron-photon interaction is evaluated using a 4th-order perturbation theory. Our findings indicate that both types of interactions cause redshifts in the gap-plasmon frequencies. However, these shifts exhibit distinct tendencies, with the electron-electron interaction producing a more significant effect and depending on the gap width, whereas the electron-photon interaction diminishes with decreasing gap size. Additionally, our research highlights the significance of incorporating a macroscopic polarizability correction, which significantly impacts the understanding of plasmon behavior.

Type theory based on intuitionistic, piecemeal construction of mathematical proofs has a long-standing association with normalization. However, the introduction of dependent types compromises the normalizing property of type theory. This complication arose with the development of the Calculus of Constructions, a foundational theory that incorporates advanced type constructs such as universes with positive equality proof requirements. To address this issue, we adapt a robust normalization approach that accommodates partial and flawed type isomorphisms during the reduction process. This strategy enables the efficient elimination of unsatisfiable types, even with the presence of non-normalizable types and circular references in type definitions. As a result, this approach facilitates the development of reliable and certifiable code generation for the core types of the Calculus of Constructions.

A fundamental understanding of topological quantum states relies on the concept of symmetry-protected edges in models like the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger. This model features two distinct object representations - either atomic sites or lattice sites - which correspond to different universes of description. In our investigation, we switch between these representations, considering both their physical and matricular aspects. When we use the site description, the model includes a specific symmetry-breaking term that explains the edge state within the framework of topology. Conversely, the atomic description views the edge state as a localized defect, separate from topological classifications. Our research demonstrates that both interpretations are equally valid, yet they yield distinct results regarding topological properties. Ultimately, our findings emphasize the importance of clear language in describing physical systems and the caution against mixing physical and matricular languages.

This paper discusses the distinctive characteristics and advantages of using mixture models with a finite number of components. We examine how variational approximation can make complex models more manageable by incorporating techniques from probabilistic geometry and the theory of Choquet integral. This leads to a more accessible presentation of Bayesian inference as a data-driven method that can handle non-convergence issues. We also illustrate the precise connections between mixture models and the mentioned mathematical frameworks, highlighting the role of convex optimization in accurately estimating model parameters. Furthermore, we establish a link between the geometric interpretation of mixture models and the algebraic representation of convex functions, which facilitates a deeper understanding of these models. Finally, we emphasize the essential role of robust statistics in furthering our knowledge of complex datasets, citing famous examples such as the stock market, social networks, and genetic data, which often exhibit similar statistical characteristics.

We have derived the full dual-loop correction for type-IIB supergravity in the AdS$_5\times$S$^5$ background, utilizing the conformal field theory perspective. By accounting for perturbative contributions from massless fields in AdS$_5$, and non-perturbative effects from BPS states in S$^5$, we have calculated the dual-loop correction to the graviton self-energy at zero energy and angular momentum. This result agrees with predictions from CFT, which can determine the AdS$_5$ part of the supergravity correlation function up to dual-loop order. Furthermore, we have verified that the Nambu-Goto string partition function, describing IIB strings on S$^5$, accurately includes non-perturbative BPS contributions up to dual-loop order. Building upon this understanding, we have gained insight into how the AdS$_5$ portion of the supergravity correlation function is connected to the S$^5$ partition function through the use of boundary conditions.

Concurrent memory allocation on GPUs is complicated due to two requirements: having fast, parallel memory allocation like static allocation, and being able to handle memory fragmentation like dynamic allocation. In object-oriented programming, objects are allocated based on classes, which can result in memory fragmentation caused by unevenly sized objects, further exacerbating the problem when combining it with parallel development. This paper introduces DynaSOAr, a concurrent dynamic memory allocator tailored for object-oriented development on GPUs, allowing for efficient memory use and minimal fragmentation. By assigning a specific memory range, or "segment", to each class, DynaSOAr can allocate memory quickly and efficiently, either from a pool of small blocks or a larger block corresponding to the size of the class, depending on the size of the memory required. This approach is then compared to other methods of memory allocation in programs that demonstrate good memory usage, and the potential for further optimization is also discussed.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a diverse set of operators, including those generated by the Calderón-Zygmund operators and the fractional integral operator, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Additionally, the article examines the boundedness of the commutators of these operators on the same space. Furthermore, specific applications are considered for operators like the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator, the Calderón-Zygmund singular integral operators, and the Calderón-Zygmund operators with weights, demonstrating their boundedness or failure of boundedness.

A new theoretical approach is presented that enables the description of superconducting proximitized local magnetic impurities and their dimers within the framework of a real-space, spin-polarized Keldysh technique. By incorporating the YSR states and interacting with a superconducting host metal, the formalism includes the effects of both spin exchange and asymmetry. With explicit applications to manganese adatoms and dimers on the Nb(110) surface, the theoretical framework is put to the test. The findings are compared with experimental data, and the sensitivity of the calculated quantities is examined in relation to the accuracy of the atomic and molecular magnetic exchange interactions. The developed approach is particularly useful for analyzing magnetic monomer and dimer molecules in proximity to superconducting hosts, involving strong hybridization with host electrons, and requiring a precise understanding of proximate spin exchange and asymmetry interactions.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural networks to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit network, allowing it to focus on distinguishing between foreground and background objects. By leveraging the Fourier series, FourierMask can produce more precise mask predictions and extends the application of Fourier transformation in the context of instance segmentation beyond current limitations.

This note provides a proof for thefulness of locally area-increasing mappings from a bounded domain in R^n to R^m, where n and m satisfy the condition m >= 2n-1. Furthermore, the proof extends to certain non-locally area-increasing mappings under certain volume constraints, demonstrating the possibility of these mappings to R^m having a full range.

The proposed concept of cloud imaging from space involves a method to estimate the accuracy of images obtained, even when clouds are fully opaque. The approach, which can be used for either two-dimensional optical thickness measurements or for determining the angular extent of visible cloud regions, is being considered for incorporation into a future satellite system. To test this method, researchers used data from the MISR and MODIS satellite instruments, taking into account factors such as the sun's position, the temperature difference between clouds and surroundings, and the presence of cloud boundaries. The results indicate that the technique is capable of providing an objective accuracy assessment for cloud imaging, and this study provides the underlying scientific justification for this capability.

This research proposes a new concept to significantly improve ion thruster efficiency by utilizing a chirp coded radio frequency field to create a self-inducing transparency effect within a plasma channel. A two-dimensional model incorporating the superposition of linear wave equations has been utilized to analyze this phenomenon, resulting in the emergence of a relativistic ion beam propagation mechanism. Numerical simulations indicate that this approach may enable ion thrusters to achieve specific impulses in the range of 5000 seconds, surpassing current state-of-the-art ion thrusters by a factor of ten.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the interior temperatures of these planets using various radiative-convective models, researchers found that TOI-712 bat (the Earth-sized candidate) might have conditions suitable for life, while the other planets have temperatures that are too low. This discovery provides valuable insights into the formation and development of young stars and their planetary systems.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile-TiO$_{2}$.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have the same arrangement within the TiO$_{2}$ lattice, but differ in their energy levels -  carbon forms a pair of bond-centered sites, whereas nitrogen forms an anti-bonding site.  Both defects displayed spin polarization, with nitrogen exhibiting a more stable anti-bonding state when compared to carbon.  Notably, nitrogen maintained its anti-bonding characteristics when placed in interstitial locations, whereas carbon only exhibited this arrangement when placed in a smaller 32-atom supercell.  Furthermore, we found that nitrogen doping could reduce the bandgap of TiO$_{2}$ from 1.29 eV to 0.45 eV, potentially enhancing its photocatalytic properties.

Top quark production via an elastic process, such as $p p \to t \bar{t} u \bar{u}$, has significant implications for beyond Standard Model physics, particularly in scenarios involving large extra dimensions or new gauge bosons. To facilitate detection of this production process, we propose using data from the Large Hadron Collider to search for $t \to u \gamma$. This analysis would involve searching for events consisting of two photons, four jets, and missing transverse momentum, with the assumption that the system originates from a single source. Following the elimination of irreducible di-photon top quark events, approximately 20-40 event candidates would remain, which would be sufficient to establish a signal at a 4-sigma confidence level with as few as 300 detected events. Furthermore, we outline the strategy for identifying the elastic $t \bar{t} u \bar{u}$ production process by looking for the sequence of particles energies, spin correlations, and angular distributions, which would enable us to determine the elastic $t \bar{t}$ contribution with reasonable precision, even if it represents a small fraction of the $t \bar{t}$ production.

Previous research has shown that the intra-cluster medium's turbulence exhibits scale-dependent characteristics. To further investigate this phenomenon, this paper analyzes potential biases in the data resulting from measurement inaccuracies when using X-ray surface brightness fluctuations as a probe. These inaccuracies arise from the combination of temperature and density fluctuations affecting X-ray emission, which are not accounted for in the standard methodology. While previous work assumed that the gas temperature varies smoothly, this paper models temperature fluctuations statistically. It considers two scenarios: temperature fluctuations that are correlated with the global cluster trend and temperature fluctuations that are randomly variations. For the first scenario, the estimated structure functions are biased by the squaring of the amplitude of fluctuations. In contrast, the second scenario leads to an unbiased estimation of structure functions. This distinction implies that future observations should be designed to gather additional data on temperature fluctuations to gain a deeper understanding of the intra-cluster medium's turbulence.

We investigate an upper richness property associated with Ramsey theory, specifically focusing on its behavior within distinct components of an infinite graph. Our analysis reveals that in an arbitrary infinite graph, each component satisfies a particular upper richness level that is equivalent to a specific ruf property. However, we also demonstrate that there is an upper limit to the complexity of such properties; further, this limit can be achieved; in addition, this achievable upper limit can be attained through a specific, highly symmetric configuration.

Located within the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation, where molecular material is concentrated. Recent studies have shown that the CMZ's mass distribution is not uniform, with a notable alignment in the direction perpendicular to the Galactic Center. To quantify this anisotropic arrangement, a new statistical approach was developed, involving two-dimensional correlation functions. By utilizing this method, the degree of mass clustering in the CMZ was determined for two different orientations: one parallel and the other perpendicular to the Galactic Center. The results revealed that the CMZ exhibits more significant self-clustering in the direction perpendicular to the Galactic Center, with a value of 1.4, indicating a substantial mass configuration over 30pc in radius and 10pc in width. Furthermore, this anisotropic arrangement was found to be a general feature of massive star-forming regions throughout the galaxy.

A potentially life-threatening condition called bilateral facial paralysis, also known as Bell's palsy, can cause sudden and painless facial weakness on one side. It is essential to treat this condition within 72 hours of symptom onset for optimal results. However, early diagnosis can be challenging due to the varying severity of symptoms in different individuals. Current methods of diagnosis involve a physical examination by a neurologist or primary care physician. There is a need for non-invasive and accurate systems that can detect Bell's palsy from video recordings of a person's eyes. Previous studies have demonstrated the efficacy of eye-centered systems in identifying this condition; nevertheless, they have primarily focused on static images rather than dynamic video. In contrast, our proposed model, a sequential eye-centered Bell's palsy detection network (SEBNet), leverages convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to accurately diagnose Bell's palsy from videos. By utilizing attention mechanisms, SEBNet prioritizes crucial visual elements for classification, whereas reinforcement learning (RL) is used to enhance the model's overall performance. Compared to the existing eye-centered static model, SEBNet exhibits superior results on the newly introduced dataset consisting of eye-only video recordings.

The quantum electrodynamics in su(2) invariant space, known as sQED, is a highly regarded model for studying spin phenomena using quantum simulations. Researchers have previously outlined the basic setup for quantum simulations of sQED using the Husimi Q-function, which effectively maps the complex Hilbert space into a real one, but only at the zero-photon state. However, this approach has a significant drawback in that it destroys the quantum nature of light. In our work, we deviate from this method and propose the use of multilevel qutrits with laser driving to improve the sound detection in quantum simulations of sQED. By adopting the Poincaré section method, which utilizes simplified, quasi-classical descriptions of quantum systems, we are able to accurately model this system despite only having partial knowledge of its quantum state. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of this system by successfully retrieving sQED's physical phenomena, including both stable and unstable photon dynamics, as well as the emission spectra of excited spin states.

The interaction between an ultra-high intensity laser and a thin polarized foil target is examined in the context of strong field quantum electrodynamics. When the degree of circular polarization in the photoelectron spike exceeds 1%, it indicates an observable effect. To move this from a laboratory-based observation to a detectable polarization in positron beams, our analysis reveals that an increase in positron yield by two orders of magnitude is necessary. This could be achieved by using a bunched target in conjunction with a grazing incidence of the laser. As a result, we propose the development of a novel technique using a polarized foil target in combination with an ultra-high intensity laser. If realized, this could facilitate the generation of densely packed, polarized positron beams.

Let G be a finite group with the diameter d defined as the minimum number n of distinct elements eG such that 1+n^2 equals the largest eigenvalue of its adjacency matrix \lambda_{max}(G). In this work, we determine or limit from above d for many well-known types of groups through various fields, including number theory (for nilpotent groups), linear algebra (for solvable groups), and the study of quadratic forms. Specifically, we prove that the diameter of a solvable group is always less than or equal to 2*sqrt(2*n), a nilpotent group has a diameter less than or equal to 2*sqrt(n), and a p-group of rank r has a diameter less than or equal to 2*sqrt(r)*sqrt[p-1].

This research develops a temperature detection microchip with a built-in
temperature sensor, which provides a digital output indicating whether the
temperature has risen or fallen. The design caters to various application
temporal ranges, featuring a 32-bit finite state machine (FSM) to convert the
sensor's analog output into a digital temperature reading. The proposed FSM
architecture offers enhanced precision at lower temperatures and is capable of
functioning across a broad temperature range of -40{\deg}C to 120{\deg}C.
Furthermore, it can be designed for different allowable temperature ranges.
The implemented 32-bit FSM temperature sensor, utilizing a 65nm CMOS process,
demonstrates exceptionally small size, with a minimal area of 0.021mm^2, and is
capable of converting temperature to digital output in 10ms. The design
provides a relatively low power consumption of 200nW when converting a full
temperature cycle and 100nW for repeated conversions within the same
temperature range.

The long-term stability of magnetic fields in stars is a topic of ongoing research, especially given the intricate relationship between magnetic fields, mechanical mixing, and nuclear reactions in stellar interiors.  Utilizing the WKB approximation, this study assesses the stability of magnetic fields in stably burning hydrogen in main-sequence stars.  For non-uniformly distributed magnetic flux, the presence of global mode truncation hinders the determination of stability.  However, local instabilities are identified at high latitudes.  In contrast, uniformly distributed magnetic flux allows for a more nuanced analysis, revealing instability in regions near the convective envelope and at high latitudes.  These local instabilities have the potential to impact global magnetic field stability.  A three-dimensional simulation of a solar-type star confirms the findings of this study, with the most unstable global mode corresponding to $m=\pm 1$ at latitudes of approximately $\pm 20.6^\circ$.  Given the short timescales associated with these instabilities, stars with densely packed inner cores, such as $\eta$ Cephei, may have magnetic fields that change over time.  This has implications for core rotation measurements based on nuclear diffusion rates.

Using the functional renormalization group (FRG), researchers study the changes in a quantum field theory as a parameter is varied. The FRG flow equations resemble those found in the renormalization group within perturbative QCD. A notable difference exists, however, as the former can be applied to interacting fermions beyond perturbation theory. Despite this capability, the accuracy of the FRG approach for describing physical phenomena has not been thoroughly validated, particularly in regions far from the physical parameters used in its development. In this study, we evaluate the precision of the FRG method for renormalization group flows in a simple, zero-dimensional quantum field theory known as the O(N) model, in which a single type of fermion interacts with itself in a variety of ways. By comparing the predictions made using the FRG flow equations and exact mathematical solutions for this model, we determine the errors associated with the use of the Wilsonian flow equations. These errors are shown to decrease with an increase in certain large numbers, which are essential properties of physical systems and often serve as scales in the theory. These large numbers include the number of symmetry generators (N), the number of fermion components (2S + 1), and the ratio of the fermion mass to its characteristic infrared value, denoted by $m/M$. In the case of the O(N) model, the precision of the Wilsonian approach is accurate to within 1% for values of these parameters that are relevant to physical

Music comprehension, where systems interpret musical compositions, has seen significant advancements in recent years. However, existing approaches focus largely on literal interpretations, neglecting the deeper emotional and imaginative aspects of music. Inspired by advancements in visual question answering and the richness of musical experiences, we propose a novel concept called meta inquiry for music. This new framework encourages the development of innovative models that can delve deeper into musical compositions, fostering a more immersive understanding of music. In line with this framework, we introduce Pied Piper, a cutting-edge model capable of engaging in complex musical conversations and captivating performances. Through our experiments, Pied Piper exhibits an uncanny ability to entertain and impress audiences with its musical compositions, demonstrating superior creativity and practicality in multiple settings.

We provide a theoretical framework for objects known as differentiable stacks that can be thought of as a combination of geometric structures, including foliations and groupoids. This framework is then applied to a specific type of geometric object called the quotient groupoid, which helps to simplify the structure of discrete objects, such as finite groups, within the context of smooth geometry.

A massive infrared dark cloud, capable of giving birth to a high-mass star, is in its early stages of core formation.  Observations of the dust and gas in this process are critical to understanding how high-mass star formation begins.  We used the Submillimeter Wave Astrophone Bank (SMALL) array at the Submillimeter Telescope to study the structure and velocity of dust and gas in the Dragon infrared dark cloud.  Our data show that the cloud is in an incipient stage of collapse, with an irregular shape and mixed molecular gas and ionization.  The core of the cloud is decreasing in size and has a distinct velocity.  There is also a smaller, rotating disk within the core.  The parameters of this system are similar to those of the OMC-2 region, which is thought to be giving birth to a high-mass star.  The Dragon infrared dark cloud offers a unique opportunity to study the early stages of high-mass star formation.

Godel modal logics have been found useful in analyzing pregnancy-related complications and other situational dependencies. However, the lack of a clear understanding of their semantic foundation has limited the development of Godel modal logics. By examining various definitions of validity for Godel pretables, especially those based on maximal consistent sets and hybrid algebras, this work sheds light on the relational structures and algebras underlying Godel modal logics, including their correspondence with Kripke semantics and the preservation of validity under Godelization. Furthermore, this research enables the straightforward development of algebras and relational structures for controlled expansions of Godel modal logics, such as those involving distributivity and S5 axioms.

LiDAR technology enables the creation of detailed 3D environments in various settings, including autonomous navigation, culture heritage preservation, and forestry management. Researchers often extract valuable information from these datasets for subsequent tasks. Nonetheless, the scalability and practical applications of such methodologies are hindered by their reliance on labeled training data. In this work, we investigate the potential of leveraging machine learning tools to uncover meaningful relationships within 3D point clouds, thereby enabling the prediction of target variables without the need for explicit labeling. Specifically, we utilized U-Net, a popular semantic segmentation model, to predict target variables (e.g., forest species, ages, and densities) directly from 3D LiDAR data. In our experiments, we demonstrated that this approach outperformed baseline methods using traditional feature extraction techniques. Furthermore, our results indicated that deep learning architectures can effectively capture relevant information from 3D LiDAR data, leading to accurate predictions of the target variables.

We derive explicit formulas for computing posterior means and variances in Gaussian process regression when the input data is two-dimensionally sampled. We demonstrate that using a spherical domain instead of a rectangular one does not inherently complicate these calculations. To this end, we first establish the formula for calculating the moments of a Gaussian field on the sphere, and this leads to an efficient algorithm for modeling real data. To evaluate the method's performance, we compare it to an alternative approach using a Gaussian process emulator.

The observation of extremely high-energy cosmic particles remains a pivotal area of study in astronomy. Our research suggests utilizing neutrino observations to determine if high-energy cosmic sources are spatially associated. By combining neutrino data with ultra-high-energy cosmic particle arrival locations, we can pinpoint potential source areas and accurately account for directional biases. Our statistical approach, tailored to handle gigaelectronvolts neutrino energies, reveals no significant connection between neutrino and ultra-high-energy cosmic particle arrival locations. Nonetheless, we find that UHECR sources are significantly linked at 90% confidence when considering only spatial correlations within the neutrino sphere.

The flow of liquid foams is significantly influenced by two main factors: viscosity and surface tension. However, the interplay between these factors is complicated by the unique properties of foams, which possess both liquid and solid characteristics. In particular, the behavior of thin liquid films within the foam demands careful consideration. While previous research has focused on the relationship between surface tension and the geometry of these films, our study reveals that the coefficient of friction between the liquid films also plays a crucial role in determining the behavior of the films. By precisely controlling the texture of a specific substrate, we observe a notable increase in the friction experienced by the films, which in turn affects the overall flow of the foam. Through a combination of experiments and numerical simulations, we identify the physical mechanisms driving this increase in friction and demonstrate that it results in a substantial reduction of the films' thickness and the emergence of new geometric patterns. Ultimately, our findings offer a broader insight into the complex interplay between surface tension, viscosity, and friction in liquid foams, which has implications for the design of efficient drainage systems and the better understanding of flow dynamics in porous media.

This report outlines the top results achieved by our team in the 2019 ISIC challenge, which focused on using imaging data to identify skin carcinoma. The task required the differentiation of melanoma, the most deadly form of skin cancer, from other types of skin lesions. Unfortunately, medical professionals face a difficult challenge in this area – according to estimates, about 10% of melanoma patients survive beyond five years, whereas the survival rate for non-melanoma skin cancer is essentially 100%. The key lies in early detection of melanoma. Despite the importance of this task, recent approaches have relied heavily on conventional hand-engineered features instead of more effective deep learning techniques. Our solution employed a deep learning algorithm, combining a simple dataset configuration with the use of outlier detection to identify redundant samples, allowing us to efficiently train a highly accurate melanoma detection model from a relatively small dataset.

The interplay between surface tension and rotation in a confined cell, where the inner wall is inclined at an angle $\phi$, leads to an intriguing phenomenon when a foreign liquid with lower viscosity and surface tension than the filled liquid is introduced through a hole in the center. This results in the formation of a mix of radial and circular folds in the foreign liquid, which can accommodate a much larger amount of liquid than would be possible if the cell were not rotated. This difference highlights the effect of rotation on instability modes, with (f/Im)_{\text{crit}} decreasing by approximately half when the angle $\phi$ shifts from $90^\circ$ to $45^\circ$. A similar reduction in (Ga/Im)_{\text{crit}} is observed as the angle $\phi$ changes from $90^\circ$ to $45^\circ$. Furthermore, we have the relationship $\beta \propto \text{Co}^{-0.4}$, and the fact that the curvature of the finger at its tip is determined by the viscosity ratio rather than the ratio of curvatures in the nonrotating situation. This means that the tip of the finger is more closely aligned with the inner wall of the cell as the rate of rotation increases. This alignment can be used as a nondestructive method to determine whether a particular configuration is producing radial or circular instability.

Initially, microstate analysis was proposed to examine the dynamics of quantum systems, but their unique property poses a significant challenge. Specifically, it's difficult to compare initial and final microstates due to their varying phase space volumes, a problem that persists even in simple expansion scenarios. To overcome this obstacle, we've developed a new theoretical approach utilizing Hamiltonian paths, effectively allowing the comparison of these states in any phase space dimension. Applying this method to the expansion case reveals that the observed divergence is merely an artifact of system reorganization, and our results demonstrate that the proposed approach is more accurate than conventional methods.

Scientists have long been analyzing interstellar molecular spectra using radio astronomy, and recent observations of the TMC-1 region using the ATLASArchive have led to the discovery of two previously unknown ethynyl cyclopentadiene variants, CCHC$_5$H$_4$ and CNC$_5$H$_4$. By employing a novel approach that incorporates a parameterized molecular Hamiltonian for cy c lopentadiene, researchers have successfully assigned the frequencies corresponding to these two new cyclopentadiene derivatives, as well as three already known variants. In addition, scientists have determined the column densities of all five cyclopentadiene derivatives, and upon comparing them to related benzene derivatives, have inferred abundance ratios of approximately 0.05 for CCH and 1.4 for CN, both of greater intensity than their benzene counterparts. The findings suggest that the cyclopentadiene ring can withstand high energy photon fields with minimal distortion, and thus offer valuable insights for interpreting spectral data, particularly in regions heavily exposed to radiation.

The current attention-based neural machine translation (NMT) paradigm employs a unified attention mechanism that equally distributes attention across all source sentences in a batch. However, this uniform distribution may lead to poor performance when processing lengthy source sentences. To address this issue, we introduce a look-forward attention mechanism that leverages contextual information to select relevant parts of the source sentence one word at a time. This attention mechanism allows the model to focus on parts of the sentence that have not been processed yet, thereby avoiding premature focus on unnecessary sentence components. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our look-forward attention mechanism enhances translation accuracy for lengthy source sentences and extends the benefits to other sequence-to-sequence tasks like text generation.

The concept of translational research has long been recognized in fields like medicine and social sciences, where complex problems require collaboration between distinct disciplines. Unfortunately, the benefits of translational research are less pronounced in computer science due to the absence of a clear method for cross-disciplinary project development. As a result, the growth of computer science is often hindered and its potential for addressing global challenges untapped. To bridge this gap, we propose a new approach, called translational development, which involves taking a theoretical computer science concept and creating a practical application out of it. To illustrate the value of this approach, we used the example of grid computing, which failed to live up to its expected potential despite being theoretically sound. By reaping the benefits of translational development, the field of computer science can contribute more effectively to solving the world's most pressing problems.

A combined dark fluid model has been proposed which incorporates a dissipative dark energy component and a non-interacting dark matter part, utilizing a scalar field with an exponential potential. The model's cosmological parameters are found to be in line with the constraints of the Planck satellite, and a thorough analysis of the model's dynamics through the use of a numerical method, is presented. The results show that the model exhibits a similar evolutionary path to the $\Lambda$-Cold Dark Matter model, and its predictions for the density profile of galaxy rotations and the distribution of galaxy masses are consistent with empirical findings. Furthermore, the model predicts a relationship between the Hubble constant and the matter density parameter, $\Omega_m$, which could be verified through upcoming large-scale galaxy surveys.

In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for a future where lifelong learning and skill acquisition will be increasingly essential.  Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One understudied aspect of curiosity is its link to peer interactions.  Our study introduces a theoretical framework that combines cognitive and social factors to explain how peers can inspire curiosity through observation, and how this relationship affects academic motivation and performance.  This framework is the basis for the curiosity indices that we developed and tested in our study, which utilized a mixed-methods design to examine curiosity in a college learning skills course.  Our results show that students' initial levels of curiosity are high, but they tend to decline over time.  In addition, we found that curiosity peaks after group work and class discussions.  Our data also indicate that curiosity is a robust predictor of academic motivation and performance, and our findings are consistent across both quantitative and qualitative analyses.  Our study provides valuable insights for educators on designing effective learning environments that foster curiosity through peer interactions, and it paves the way for further research on the dynamics of curiosity in learning environments.

Gaussian processes have emerged as a key tool for analyzing and predicting data trends, especially in high-dimensional spaces.  Their success, however, is largely confined to isotropic settings and craters when it comes to modeling anisotropic data.  This paper introduces a novel approach, based on the Mat\'ern family, that adapts Gaussian processes to effectively capture complex anisotropies present in data by incorporating a new set of parameters that characterize the Gaussian process's smoothness and spatial decay.  By demonstrating the Mat\'ern Gaussian process's anisotropic modeling capabilities and showing that it subsumes traditional Gaussian processes, we show that our approach's anisotropic parameters are determinable through integrated squared errors.  We also introduce an innovative technique for scaling Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to large datasets by only requiring a small random sample size, which significantly boosts their computational efficiency while maintaining prediction accuracy.  Through extensive experiments, we show that our approach outperforms the status quo in multiple settings and easily integrates with popular Bayesian optimization frameworks, enabling the solution of high-dimensional, anisotropic objective functions.

The growing use of ridesharing services has generated substantial digital footprints, enabling researchers to improve urban infrastructure management through data-driven methods. A proposed framework for detecting urban roads by analyzing ridesharing data is presented, along with a technique to identify and remove false positives. The effectiveness of this approach is verified through the collection of GPS and accelerometer data from 8000 rides in New York City and a comparison with existing methods demonstrates its superiority, with a reported 20% reduction in errors.

Our research delves into the significance of examining the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for better understanding neutrino and dark energy. The J/ψ particle primarily breaks down into muon and antimuon, but it can also transform into other forms of energy. To understand the neutrino sector, we use the J/ψ invisible decay into a single neutrino, taking into account the most significant loop processes involving electroweak and dark matter particles. In contrast, to understand dark energy, we focus on the J/ψ invisible decay into a single particle, with contributions from a scalar field and vector field, with a further contribution from a vector field involving neutrino-antineutrino mixing. The most significant loop processes for the neutrino sector involve the weak force and the interaction between neutrinos and dark matter, with large diagonal form factor contributions, indicating the need for a comprehensive understanding of the neutrino sector through the J/ψ invisible decay. In the dark energy sector, the most significant contributions come from a scalar field with a negative mass term and the weak force, with the latter resulting in extremely small contributions. The dark photon field contributes neutrino non-standard interactions, with the need for separate evaluations for each neutrino flavor. The total and differential cross-sections of the J/ψ invisible decay have distinct features when considering the most significant loop processes involving dark matter particles. The current experimental limits on the J/ψ invisible decay width are not sufficient to make notable constraints on

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

This work introduces the multivariate functional singular spectrum examination (MFSE) for analyzing multivariate functional time series data across distinct dimensional domains. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSE through simulated scenarios and real-world applications, highlighting its utility in identifying temporal variation, assessing dimensionality, and performing component analysis for multivariate functional data.

Deep learning-based automated driving emergency assistance systems are now commonplace. However, their reliance on neural network technology for sensory data interpretation creates an instability issue when confronted with unforeseen events. This paper delves into the source of this instability by examining the structural and functional aspects of these neural networks. Specifically, it investigates how the use of convolutional neural networks and linear classification models contributes to their inability to accurately predict driving outcomes from raw sensory data. Furthermore, it highlights the inherent bias present in dataset collections that these systems are trained from. Rather than proposing new methods for predicting driving outcomes, the paper presents a theoretical framework explaining why AES systems are prone to instability and also susceptible to significant overresponses. It then outlines two potential mitigation strategies: first, the use of middle-layer features as input instead of raw sensory data; and second, the implementation of dataset cleaning processes to remove inconsistent data points. If successful, these approaches could provide a foundation for developing more reliable and efficient AES systems.

This study establishes an asymptotic formula for the number of times a random walk with zero mean and finite variance spends time above a threshold before returning to the starting point. Additionally, a condition is set to ensure the walk does not immediately return to the starting point.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to study plasma interactions and probe plasma characteristics. A high-frequency plasma generator is used for plasma creation, operating in two modes: an RF mode and a helicon mode. This study focuses on the helicon mode, which produces a linearly polarized electromagnetic wave at 27.5 MHz to generate plasma via an RF antenna. To verify the effectiveness of this plasma generator, researchers utilized a range of diagnostic tools, including interferometry, a flux probe, and a Langmuir probe. Their findings show that in the helicon mode, a 1 A current results in 300 A of electron tube current and a 13 A/m^2 plasma density at a 0.58 V tongue potential. Additionally, a 1.36 m long plasma column with a 0.1 m diameter is observed.

This research paper presents a novel microbial biopesticide model, which incorporates the impact of introducing a new pathogen to a harmful insect population and the simultaneous release of biopesticides through infected insect dispersal. The model is examined in two distinct environmental scenarios: a closed system and an open system with periodic insect population fluctuations. In both scenarios, the required conditions for the model's steady-state solutions, which indicate the extinction or persistence of the biopesticide, are determined. Furthermore, the model's asymptotic behavior in both scenarios is demonstrated numerically. Additionally, the study investigates the efficacy of the biopesticide in a system representing the Philippines' climatic conditions.

In analyzing pathology slides, nucleus segmentation is a crucial preliminary step.
Existing methods have achieved promising results but often struggle with accurately
identifying nuclei due to varying sizes and irregular shapes of nuclei, especially
when they overlap, are out of focus, or located near image boundaries.
To address these challenges, this paper introduces a novel dual-stage network,
W-Net, for nucleus segmentation in histology images.
Initially, a coarse-scale stage uses a deep fully convolutional network to generate
a coarse mask, while a fine-scale stage refines the result using a high-resolution
image and coarse mask to produce the final output.
Experiments conducted on two public datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art
performance for nucleus segmentation.

Let's consider a field of characteristic not two and denote it by $k$. We establish the converse of Hilbert's Satz 90 for the special orthogonal group $SO_{2n+1}(D)$ and the symplectic group $Sp_{2n}(D)$, where $D$ is a central division algebra over $k$ with a finite rank. This result remains valid when $k$ has a characteristic of three. Furthermore, we prove that every $k$-linear map $\phi: D \to D$ that preserves the respective quadratic forms can be expressed as an inner automorphism of $D$. If the characteristic of $k$ is not three, we demonstrate that such a map $\phi$ can be written as a product of the Frobenius map and an inner automorphism of $D$.

A graph G is considered to have an detectable i-th iterated line graph if (G,i) belongs to a specific set defined by the hamiltonian route index λ. This paper examines the properties of this definition, specifically focusing on G's characteristics when it satisfies the condition for any i, and also identifies specific classes of graphs that have detectable, i-th iterated line graphs for various values of i.

Cell death through pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to SARS-CoV-2 transmission by facilitating the virus's spread. Unfortunately, pyroptosis's complex cellular mechanisms make it difficult to model mathematically. To address this challenge, we develop a novel approach by simplifying pyroptosis as a autonomous cell death process and incorporate it into a modified Gli1-STAT3 circuit that governs inflammation. By analyzing the resulting system, we identify key parameters that determine whether a solitary infected cell survives, dies through pyroptosis, or dies through other forms of inflammation. Our analysis reveals that these parameters significantly influence the likelihood of pyroptosis-induced cell death transmission. Given the limited understanding of these parameters, we examine their sensitivity in our model. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that reducing the rate at which the STAT3 protein is activated could significantly lower the probability of pyroptosis-induced cell death transmission. Given the role of STAT3 in inflammation, our model provides a basis for investigating the impact of anti-inflammatory interventions on reducing viral transmission.

External influences can significantly impact reinforcement learning models by introducing unanticipated fluctuations and steering them away from achieving optimal goals. This concept is the focus of this research, which aims to remove any external impacts affecting state parameters and reward signals in partially observable environments. By extending beyond previous scope, this study ventures into realms involving multiple state parameters, reward signals, and the interplay between them. It achieves this by developing a novel algorithm that identifies and eliminates any external impacts on state parameters and reward signals in reinforcement learning. This development is later combined with two exploration strategies, resulting in two hybrid variants that integrate the ability to discover and eliminate external influences with the benefits of state-based exploration. Through comprehensive simulation trials, the proposed method is found to outperform the baseline in domains affected by external factors and showcases the effectiveness of eliminating these factors through enhanced performance in certain scenarios.

A blockchain-based smart contract platform like Tezos can be seen as an advanced version of traditional digital ledgers, offering more sophisticated digital agreements whose workings mirror intricate biological processes. To ensure the accuracy of these complex contracts, a thorough validation process is crucial. By integrating refined types into the development process, programmers can pinpoint and address potential issues in their code before it's deployed on the network. This enables efficient and reliable collaboration between developers and the community in identifying and fixing errors in the code. Ultimately, this technique facilitates the seamless deployment of high-quality contracts on the Tezos network.

Deep Neural Networks have achieved remarkable performance in various image and signal processing tasks. Their underlying learning mechanisms, such as graph convolutional neural networks, remain underexplored for many users. To address this knowledge gap, we introduce an analytical approach using matched filtering techniques to illustrate the fundamental concepts of graph convolutional neural networks, making their underlying mechanics more accessible.

We take a Chern-Simons action that combines the gravitational and Yang-Mills fields, and show how it results in a simple, pure gravity theory that describes rotating black holes and solitons with "hairy" structures, for both abelian and non-abelian Yang-Mills forces. By making a specific choice of gauge, we can derive a conserved quantity that allows us to analyze these systems. We then express the conserved quantity in a new, more usable form that highlights its conserved nature. With this understanding, we can describe and calculate key properties of black hole and soliton configurations. Additionally, we are able to link the Yang-Mills field to a scalar field, and demonstrate that this relationship affects the conservation of the quantity. This, in turn, influences the possible configurations and modes of these gravitational systems.

We've developed an innovative strategy for creating extensive, interacting wall systems that separate distinct regions in a spacetime continuum. These walls have unique properties: they dynamically move, interact, and are distinct from typical cosmological structures due to their highly variable patterns of motion. Our model incorporates a non-reversible symmetry, a unique feature that has not been seen before in comprehensive wall system theories. This non-reversible aspect significantly affects the walls' behavior, causing their motion to become irregularly patterned over time. As a result, the overall spacetime continuum undergoes a complex transformation, affecting both gravitational and electromagnetic wave patterns. Our research provides the foundation for exploring the walls' fundamental characteristics and their overall impact on spacetime.

Precise detection of tissue displacement during ultrasound elastography is crucial for diagnosing various medical conditions affecting the liver, heart, and brain. However, the performance of elastography is often hindered by the limited lateral resolution of conventional ultrasound machines. To tackle this challenge, researchers have explored the potential of the virtual origin synthetic aperture (VOSA) technique. This study investigates the VOSA method's effectiveness in estimating lateral displacement in ultrasound elastography. By conducting numerical simulations and experimenting with real data, the results show that VOSA can accurately determine lateral displacement, outperforming conventional methods by achieving a 3-4 times increase in lateral resolution. Furthermore, VOSA's performance was found to be robust against different levels of displacement. This study paves the way for the integration of VOSA with ultrasound elastography, offering a precise and robust method for estimating tissue displacement.

Reasoning about and efficiently navigating through complex data structures is an essential skill for any computer science professional. As a result, teaching students abstract data types and associated algorithms is a fundamental educational goal. While algorithmic thinking can be promoted through coding exercises and problem-solving activities, many students struggle to transition from seeing implementations to crafting their own. In response, a methodical approach to creating pseudocode is introduced, one that is closely tied to a programming language based on occurrences of "demonstrations," or successful runs of an algorithm. This approach is T-learning, an iterative process involving the examination of algorithmic outputs, the creation of pseudocode based on that analysis, and a comparison of this pseudocode with an existing implementation. Through the use of a data structure such as trees, students can engage with this method, learning not just about the underlying data type and algorithms, but also how to think computationally.

This paper explores Ramsey properties within the Boolean algebras of cofinite subsets of a given infinite set, focusing on posets that are in the form of a V-shape. We identify various characteristics of this structure and establish the relevance of specific Ramsey properties. Additionally, we determine the extent to which these properties are equivalent, and we provide a comparison involving the Stone space associated with this Boolean algebra. Furthermore, we establish lower and upper bounds for the cardinality of certain sets that exhibit these Ramsey properties, and we investigate their implications.

In the context of large-scale high-dimensional data, the dynamic $k$-means clustering problem requires us to adapt and update a clustering continuously as new points are added or old points are removed. This paper addresses a key variation of this challenge, focusing on identifying all points that should be grouped together. Although previous work has established the efficiency of first-order methods in reducing the gradient of a strong convex relaxation of the dynamic $k$-means problem, these methods fail to achieve optimal dependence on the number of clusters $k$. In contrast, we present a new, efficient last-order dynamic $k$-means algorithm utilizing a direct approach that avoids the use of extrapolated averages. By leveraging this strategy, we demonstrate that our algorithm yields a significantly improved approximation guarantee, with a $k$-dependent term in the iteration cost, in addition to lower iteration and access costs. Specifically, our guarantees include an almost optimal iteration cost of $k$ times a base cost, with an important exception in the case where $k$ is very large. Furthermore, we show that our upper bound on iteration costs is almost optimal, with a small gap in mind. Building upon our results, we also introduce a new, efficient, and $k$-dependent dynamic $k$-means algorithm for streaming data, achieving a significant improvement over previous state-of-the-art methods.

We investigate a basic pursuit-evasion scenario where one advancer moves freely within a given environment, while being pursued by multiple agents whose movements are subject to randomness. We demonstrate that by employing a variety of comparison theorems, we can analyze this scenario by referencing a broader class of games that involve multiple agents competing to achieve the greatest reward. We then apply this framework to design efficient algorithms for resolving several critical issues related to the pursuit-evasion scenario, including whether cooperation can ensure success as effectively as the most successful individual strategy, and whether cooperative movements can be as successful as uncoordinated individual movements, and if so, how they can be optimized. Furthermore, we show that by utilizing a cooperative policy that prioritizes localized exploration, we can significantly improve the probability of success in narrow corridors and complex grids.

Inspired by the concept of nontransitive probabilities first described by Ian Stewart, we explore similar ideas using circular arrangements. We establish a general formula for calculating probabilities in nontransitive situations using circular permutations. Additionally, we investigate how the relationship between these probabilities can be determined from the underlying permutation data. Furthermore, we examine the connection between circular nontransitive probabilities and certain aspects of circular statistics.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the current applications of cycleGAN models are limited to dose augmentation, i.e., upgrading low-dose images to standard-dose images. To broaden their use, we propose a new AdaIN-switchable cycleGAN model that enables the enhancement of images from multiple low-dose images to a single high-quality image at a standard dose. The proposed framework involves creating a pair of super-resolution maps that transform multiple low-dose images into an intermediate image at half the standard dose, which is then converted to a single high-dose image by forming the inverse mapping. To improve training stability and enhance image details, we include an identity preservation loss and a cycle loss with a depth network. The proposed model also leverages domain confusion and adversarial loss to maintain physical consistency. In experiments, we show that the proposed model outperforms existing cycleGAN models when enhancing multiple low-dose images, achieving better PSNR and SSIM values with a significant reduction in parameters. Furthermore, compared to baseline single-image denoising models, our method delivers improved enhancement results, exceeding state-of-the-art models by 1.54 dB and 0.31 in PSNR

Recent successes in dialogue comprehension tasks have motivated the community to combine comprehension and generation in parallel for improved performance.
